docs.title: SmartMessage Documentation
docs.text:
SmartMessage is a Ruby messaging framework that separates a message from the transport that carries it. A message class declares its properties, validations, addressing and handlers; a transport moves the serialized message. The comparison the project uses is ActiveRecord: ActiveRecord keeps a model independent of the database behind it, SmartMessage keeps a message independent of the transport behind it.

This documentation describes SmartMessage 0.1.0, which requires Ruby 4.0 or newer. If you are coming from an earlier version, read Upgrading from 0.0.x first.

docs.title: Addressing
docs.text:
Every message header has three addressing fields. Their values are entity ids: Strings your application chooses, such as service names.

Field Required Meaning from yes The entity sending the message to no The intended recipient. nil means a broadcast. reply_to no Where a reply should be sent

Addressing does not change where a transport delivers a message: every subscriber of the message class on that transport receives it. Addressing is what subscription filters match on, and what handlers read.

from, to and reply_to are reserved names. They live in the header and cannot be declared as properties.

docs.title: Class defaults
docs.text:
# messages/order_message.rb
class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from     'order-service'
  to       'fulfillment-service'
  reply_to 'order-service'

  property :order_id, required: true
end

The same thing with the header block:

class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  header do
    from     'order-service'
    to       'fulfillment-service'
    reply_to 'order-service'
  end

  property :order_id, required: true
end

header at class level takes a block and nothing else; any other call raises ArgumentError.

Class defaults are inherited by subclasses. A subclass that sets its own value does not change its parent.

OrderMessage.from                # => "order-service"
OrderMessage.to_configured?      # => true
OrderMessage.reply_to_missing?   # => false
OrderMessage.reset_to            # forget this class's own value

docs.title: Per message
docs.text:
Pass addressing to new, or set it afterwards. An instance keeps its addressing in its header.

order = OrderMessage.new(order_id: 'ORD-1', to: 'express-fulfillment')

order.from                      # => "order-service"        (class default)
order.to                        # => "express-fulfillment"  (given to new)

order.to = 'backup-fulfillment'           # setter
order.to('fulfillment-eu').reply_to('eu') # with an argument: sets and returns the message

order._sm_header.to             # => "fulfillment-eu"
order.reset_to                  # back to the class default
order.to                        # => "fulfillment-service"

A message with no from (none on the class, none given) fails validation:

class PingMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  property :text
end

ping = PingMessage.new(text: 'hello')
ping.valid?                     # => false
ping.validation_errors.first    # => { property: :from, value: nil, message: "From entity ID is required ...", source: "header" }
ping.from('console').valid?     # => true

docs.title: Point to point
docs.text:
Set to. Receivers subscribe with a to: filter so that each one handles only its own messages.

OrderMessage.subscribe(to: 'fulfillment-service')

OrderMessage.new(order_id: 'ORD-1', to: 'fulfillment-service').publish

docs.title: Broadcast
docs.text:
Leave to unset. Subscribers that want only broadcasts use broadcast: true.

class MaintenanceNotice < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'ops'
  property :text, required: true
end

MaintenanceNotice.subscribe(broadcast: true)

docs.title: Request and reply
docs.text:
The requester sets reply_to; the responder addresses its reply to it.

class PriceRequest < SmartMessage::Base
  property :sku, required: true

  def self.process(message)
    PriceReply.new(sku: message.sku, cents: 1299, from: 'pricing', to: message.reply_to).publish
  end
end

A complete version of this pattern is in Examples.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: SmartMessage has four parts: message classes, an envelope codec with a serializer, transports, and a dispatcher. A message class knows what a message contains and who handles it. A transport knows how to move bytes. The envelope turns one into the other, and the dispatcher runs handlers.

docs.title: Message classes
docs.text:
A message class inherits from SmartMessage::Base (a Hashie::Dash). It declares:

  • properties, with defaults, validation and descriptions (Properties and Validation)
  • default addressing: from, to, reply_to (Addressing)
  • a schema version
  • its transport or transports, unless the global configuration supplies one (Configuration)
  • optionally, deduplication (Message Deduplication)
  • a default handler, def self.process(message) (Handlers)

Each instance carries a header (message._sm_header, a SmartMessage::Header) with these fields:

Field Meaning uuid Unique id of this message instance; used for deduplication message_class Name of the message class published_at Set when the message is built and again when it is published publisher_pid Process id of the publisher version Schema version of the message class from, to, reply_to Addressing serializer Class name of the serializer that encoded it extensions Header fields this version does not define; kept so they survive a round trip

docs.title: Envelope and serializer
docs.text:
SmartMessage::Envelope is the single codec every transport uses. On the wire a message is one flat structure: its properties plus a _sm_header entry. The serializer (SmartMessage::Serializer::Json) turns that structure into a String and back.

Decoding does not trust its input:

  • the class named in the header must be a loaded subclass of SmartMessage::Base, otherwise SmartMessage::Errors::UnknownMessageClass
  • when the payload arrived on a channel (the Redis transport has channels), the class named in the header must match that channel, otherwise SmartMessage::Errors::MessageClassMismatch
  • only declared properties are passed to the message; anything else in the payload is dropped
  • a payload that is not an envelope raises SmartMessage::Errors::DecodeError

A decoded message is not validated automatically. A handler that needs the guarantee calls message.valid? or message.validate!.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
A transport is a subclass of SmartMessage::Transport::Base. It publishes serialized messages and hands inbound payloads to its dispatcher. Each transport instance owns:

  • a serializer
  • a dispatcher (pass dispatcher: to share one between transports)
  • a circuit breaker around publishing

Four transports ship with the gem: memory, stdout, file and Redis pub/sub. They have different delivery semantics; see Transports.

docs.title: Dispatcher
docs.text: The dispatcher keeps the subscriptions of one transport. For each incoming message it finds the handlers subscribed to that message class, applies their filters, reserves the UUID when deduplication is on, and posts each handler to a bounded thread pool with its own copy of the message. See Dispatcher.

docs.title: Publishing, step by step
docs.text:
message.publish does this:

  1. validate!: raises SmartMessage::Errors::ValidationError if the message is invalid.
  2. Raises SmartMessage::Errors::TransportNotConfigured if there is no transport.
  3. Stamps published_at and publisher_pid in the header.
  4. For each transport, independently: encode the message and call the transport inside its circuit breaker. A failure is recorded in the result and the message is written to the dead letter queue with that transport's name.
  5. Returns a SmartMessage::PublishResult, or raises SmartMessage::Errors::PublishError if every transport failed.

docs.title: Receiving, step by step
docs.text:
When a transport receives a payload:

  1. Envelope.decode rebuilds the message. A payload that cannot be decoded is stored in the dead letter queue.
  2. The dispatcher looks up the subscriptions for the message class.
  3. For each subscription whose filters match:
    1. if deduplication is enabled, the UUID is reserved in that handler's queue; a UUID that is already there is skipped
    2. the handler is posted to the thread pool with a copy of the message
  4. On a pool thread, the handler runs inside its own circuit breaker.
  5. If the handler raises, or its circuit is open, the deduplication reservation is released and the message goes to the dead letter queue. Other handlers are not affected.

docs.title: Failure handling at a glance
docs.text:
What went wrong What happens Message is invalid publish raises ValidationError; nothing is sent No transport publish / subscribe raise TransportNotConfigured One of several transports fails The result is partial?; the message is dead-lettered for that transport Every transport fails publish raises PublishError; the message is dead-lettered once per transport Payload cannot be decoded Stored raw in the dead letter queue Handler raises Message dead-lettered with transport: "handler:<handler id>" Handler circuit is open Handler is not called; message dead-lettered Handler still running at shutdown timeout Handler is killed; message dead-lettered

See Dead Letter Queue and Circuit Breakers.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
SmartMessage::Stats is a thread-safe counter store. The framework counts publish per message class, and routed, processed, failed and duplicate per message class and handler.

SmartMessage::Stats.get('OrderMessage', 'publish')                              # => 12
SmartMessage::Stats.get('OrderMessage', 'OrderMessage.process', 'processed')    # => 12
SmartMessage::Stats.stat    # every counter, keys joined with "+"
SmartMessage::Stats.reset   # clear all counters

docs.title: Extension gems
docs.text: Transports for NATS, RabbitMQ, named pipes and lanet exist as separate smart_message-transport-* gems; they have not yet been updated for 0.1.0.

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
A setting is looked up in this order, and the first place that has a value wins:

  1. the message instance: message.transport(t)
  2. the message class: OrderMessage.transport(t)
  3. a parent class, nearest first (class settings are inherited)
  4. the global configuration: SmartMessage.configure { |config| config.transport = t }

There is no step 5. In particular:

  • There is no default transport. A class with no transport anywhere has none, and publishing or subscribing raises SmartMessage::Errors::TransportNotConfigured.
  • Logging is off unless configured. With no logger anywhere, nothing is logged and no file or directory is created.

What can be set where:

Setting Instance Class (inherited) Global transport(s) message.transport(t) MessageClass.transport(t) config.transport logger MessageClass.logger(l) config.logger from, to, reply_to message.from(id), or new(from: id) MessageClass.from(id) version MessageClass.version(n) deduplication ddq_size, ddq_storage, enable_deduplication! validators, property descriptions property ... description MessageClass.description(text), not inherited

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
A class reads its own value, else its nearest ancestor's. Writing a setting on a class never changes its parent or a sibling.

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport.create(:memory)   # global
end

class AppMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'my-app'
end

class AuditMessage < AppMessage
  transport SmartMessage::Transport.create(:file, file_path: 'log/audit.jsonl')
end

class LoginAudit < AuditMessage
end

AppMessage.transport.class    # => SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport   (global)
LoginAudit.transport.class    # => SmartMessage::Transport::FileTransport     (from AuditMessage)
LoginAudit.from               # => "my-app"                                    (from AppMessage)

LoginAudit.reset_transport    # forget a class's own value; the inherited one shows through

Transports are resolved when they are used, so changing the class or global transport later affects messages that already exist, unless the instance has its own.

docs.title: Instance overrides
docs.text:
message = OrderMessage.new(order_id: 'ORD-1')
message.transport(SmartMessage::Transport.create(:stdout))   # this message only
message.publish
message.reset_transport                                      # back to the class's transports

docs.title: Several transports
docs.text:
A class or an instance can have more than one transport. Pass an Array:

class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  transport [
    SmartMessage::Transport.create(:redis, namespace: 'production'),
    SmartMessage::Transport.create(:file, file_path: 'log/orders.jsonl')
  ]
end

OrderMessage.transports            # => both
OrderMessage.transport             # => the first
OrderMessage.multiple_transports?  # => true

publish sends to each and reports each outcome; subscribe subscribes on each. See Publishing.

docs.title: Global configuration
docs.text:
SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  # Dispatcher: set these before creating the transport, which reads them
  config.dispatcher_max_threads = 10
  config.dispatcher_max_queue   = 1_000
  config.shutdown_timeout       = 5

  # Transport: none by default
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport.create(:redis, namespace: 'production')

  # Logging: off by default.  See the Logging page for the accepted values.
  config.logger    = 'log/smart_message.log'
  config.log_level = :info

  # Dead letter queue file
  config.dlq_path = '/var/lib/my_app/dead_letters.jsonl'
end

A transport's dispatcher reads dispatcher_max_threads and dispatcher_max_queue when the transport is created, so a transport created before they are set keeps the defaults. transport.dispatcher.max_threads and max_queue show the limits in effect.

Setting Default Meaning transport nil A transport instance, or an Array of them, for classes that do not set their own logger nil See Logging log_level, log_format, log_include_source, log_structured_data, log_colorize, log_options unset Shape the built-in Lumberjack logger; see Logging dlq_path $SMART_MESSAGE_DLQ_PATH, else $XDG_STATE_HOME/smart_message/dead_letters.jsonl, else ~/.local/state/smart_message/dead_letters.jsonl File of the default dead letter queue; stored as an absolute path. nil or blank restores the default dispatcher_max_threads [CPU count * 2, 4].max Handler threads per dispatcher dispatcher_max_queue 1000 Handler calls that may wait for a thread shutdown_timeout 5 Seconds SmartMessage.shutdown waits when called without timeout:

The two dispatcher limits must be positive Integers and shutdown_timeout a positive number; any other value raises ArgumentError when it is assigned.

The dispatcher settings are read when a dispatcher is created (that is, when a transport is created), so configure them first.

Other entry points:

SmartMessage.configuration                 # the current configuration object
SmartMessage.configuration = saved         # replace it (useful around a test)
SmartMessage.reset_configuration!          # back to defaults; also forgets the default dead letter queue
SmartMessage.configuration.transport_configured?
SmartMessage.configuration.logger_configured?

docs.title: Per-class logger
docs.text:
class PaymentMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  logger Logger.new('log/payments.log')
end

A class logger receives the messages logged on behalf of that class (creation, publishing, subscription). Transports, the dispatcher and the dead letter queue always use the global logger.

docs.title: The config block
docs.text:
config on a message class evaluates its block in the class, which lets you group settings:

OrderMessage.config do
  transport SmartMessage::Transport.create(:memory)
  from 'order-service'
end

docs.title: In tests
docs.text:
Give each test its own state rather than sharing a server-wide default:

def setup
  @saved = SmartMessage.configuration
  SmartMessage.configuration = SmartMessage::Configuration.new
  SmartMessage.configure do |config|
    config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport.create(:memory)
    config.dlq_path  = File.join(Dir.mktmpdir, 'dead_letters.jsonl')
  end
end

def teardown
  SmartMessage.configuration = @saved
  SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.reset_default!
end

For tests against Redis, use a unique namespace: per test run. The db number does not isolate pub/sub channels.

docs.title: Dispatcher
docs.text:
SmartMessage::Dispatcher routes incoming messages to subscribed handlers. Each transport instance creates its own dispatcher unless you pass one in, so in most programs you never build a dispatcher yourself.

For each message it:

  1. finds the subscriptions for the message class
  2. drops the subscriptions whose filters do not match
  3. reserves the message UUID for each handler when deduplication is enabled, and skips handlers that have already seen it
  4. gives each remaining handler its own copy of the message and posts it to the thread pool
  5. runs the handler inside that handler's circuit breaker
  6. on failure, releases the deduplication reservation and writes the message to the dead letter queue

docs.title: The thread pool is bounded
docs.text:
Each dispatcher has one thread pool with a fixed maximum size and a bounded queue.

Setting Default Meaning config.dispatcher_max_threads [CPU count * 2, 4].max Handler threads per dispatcher config.dispatcher_max_queue 1000 Handler calls that may wait for a thread 
SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.dispatcher_max_threads = 8
  config.dispatcher_max_queue   = 200
end

Both must be positive Integers; assigning anything else (0, nil, a String) raises ArgumentError. A dispatcher reads these when it is created, so set them before you create transports. transport.dispatcher.max_threads and transport.dispatcher.max_queue report the limits in effect.

When all threads are busy and the queue is full, the thread that is delivering the message (the publisher with the memory transport, the subscriber thread with Redis, the poller with the file transport) runs the handler itself. That slows the source down instead of letting the queue grow without limit. No message is dropped.

To give one transport its own limits, build its dispatcher:

dispatcher = SmartMessage::Dispatcher.new(max_threads: 2, max_queue: 50)
transport  = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new(dispatcher: dispatcher)

Several transports can share one dispatcher the same way; they then share subscriptions, the pool, and the deduplication queues.

docs.title: Each handler gets its own copy
docs.text:
The dispatcher calls message.dup for every handler. A copy has its own header and its own nested Hashes, Arrays and Strings.

OrderMessage.subscribe { |message| message.items << 'changed by handler one' }
OrderMessage.subscribe { |message| message.items.size }   # never sees handler one's change

docs.title: Handler isolation
docs.text: A handler that raises does not stop or affect the other handlers of the same message. Its failure is logged, counted in SmartMessage::Stats as failed, and the message is dead-lettered with transport: "handler:<handler id>". An exception never escapes a pool thread.

docs.title: Shutdown
docs.text:
SmartMessage.shutdown(timeout: 10)   # => true when every handler finished in time

SmartMessage.shutdown stops every live dispatcher. Each one stops accepting work on its pool and waits for the handlers that are queued or running. The timeout is a total budget shared by all dispatchers; without an argument it is config.shutdown_timeout (default 5 seconds).

A handler that is still running when the time is up is killed. Its message is logged and written to the dead letter queue with the error Dispatcher shut down before the handler finished, so it can be replayed.

SmartMessage registers SmartMessage.shutdown once with at_exit. Call it yourself when you want to choose the moment or the timeout, or to check the result:

at_exit do
  drained = SmartMessage.shutdown(timeout: 30)
  warn 'some handlers were killed; see the dead letter queue' unless drained
end

A single dispatcher can be shut down with dispatcher.shutdown(timeout: 5).

After a shutdown the pool is closed. A message that arrives afterwards still has its handlers run, on the thread that delivers it.

Shutting down the dispatcher does not disconnect transports. Call transport.disconnect to stop a Redis subscriber or a file poller.

docs.title: Status and statistics
docs.text:
dispatcher = OrderMessage.transport.dispatcher

dispatcher.status
# => { scheduled_task_count: 12, completed_task_count: 12, queue_length: 0,
#      length: 4, in_flight: 0, running: true }

dispatcher.subscribers            # => { "OrderMessage" => [{ subscriber_id:, process_method:, filters: }, ...] }
dispatcher.circuit_breaker_stats  # => { "OrderMessage:OrderMessage.process" => { status: :closed, ... } }
dispatcher.ddq_stats              # => { "OrderMessage:OrderMessage.process" => { size: 100, ... } }

SmartMessage::Stats.get('OrderMessage', 'OrderMessage.process', 'routed')
SmartMessage::Stats.get('OrderMessage', 'OrderMessage.process', 'processed')
SmartMessage::Stats.get('OrderMessage', 'OrderMessage.process', 'failed')
SmartMessage::Stats.get('OrderMessage', 'OrderMessage.process', 'duplicate')

in_flight is the number of handler calls that have been posted and have not finished.

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
require 'smart_message'
require 'tmpdir'

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.dispatcher_max_threads = 2
  config.dispatcher_max_queue   = 10
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new
  config.dlq_path  = File.join(Dir.mktmpdir, 'dead_letters.jsonl')
end

# messages/job_message.rb
class JobMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'scheduler'
  property :seconds, required: true

  def self.process(message)
    sleep message.seconds
    puts "finished a #{message.seconds}s job"
  end
end

JobMessage.subscribe
JobMessage.new(seconds: 0.1).publish
JobMessage.new(seconds: 5).publish

drained = SmartMessage.shutdown(timeout: 1)

entry = SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.default.peek
puts <<~REPORT
  drained in time: #{drained}
  dead letters:    #{SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.default.size}
  reason:          #{entry[:error]}
REPORT

The short job finishes. The long one is killed after one second and its message is in the dead letter queue.

docs.title: Message Filtering
docs.text:
A subscription can carry filters on the header's addressing fields. The dispatcher checks them for each incoming message and calls the handler only when they match.

Filters are applied in the subscriber's process, after the transport has delivered the message. They reduce what a handler sees, not what travels over the transport.

MessageClass.subscribe(handler = nil, from: nil, to: nil, broadcast: nil, &block)
Filter Accepts Matches when from: String, Regexp, or an Array of them the header's from equals a String or matches a Regexp to: String, Regexp, or an Array of them the header's to equals a String or matches a Regexp broadcast: true the header's to is nil

Any other filter value raises ArgumentError at subscribe time.

docs.title: How filters combine
docs.text:
• No filters: the handler gets every message of the class.
  • from: must match when it is given.
  • to: and broadcast: are alternatives: when either is given, at least one of them must match.

So subscribe(from: 'billing', to: 'me', broadcast: true) means: from billing, and either addressed to me or addressed to nobody.

A message with to: nil never matches a to: filter, and a message with from: nil never matches a from: filter.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# messages/alert_message.rb
class AlertMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  property :text, required: true

  def self.process(message)
    puts "#{message.from} -> #{message.to || 'all'}: #{message.text}"
  end
end

# Exact sender
AlertMessage.subscribe(from: 'payment-service')

# Any of several senders
AlertMessage.subscribe(from: %w[admin monitoring])

# Pattern
AlertMessage.subscribe(from: /\Apayment-/)

# Strings and patterns together
AlertMessage.subscribe(from: ['admin', /\Asystem-/])

# Addressed to this service
AlertMessage.subscribe(to: 'order-service')

# Addressed to this service, or broadcast
AlertMessage.subscribe(to: 'order-service', broadcast: true)

# Broadcasts only
AlertMessage.subscribe(broadcast: true)

# From admins, to any production service
AlertMessage.subscribe(from: /\Aadmin-/, to: /-prod\z/)

docs.title: Several subscriptions on one class
docs.text:
Each subscribe call with a block, proc or lambda adds a separate handler with its own filters:

AlertMessage.subscribe(broadcast: true)      { |message| Dashboard.show(message.text) }
AlertMessage.subscribe(to: 'on-call')        { |message| Pager.page(message.text) }
AlertMessage.subscribe(from: /\Asecurity-/)  { |message| SecurityLog.append(message.to_h) }

A message that matches several subscriptions is delivered to each of them.

A handler named by a String ("Class.method", including the default "AlertMessage.process") is identified by that String. Subscribing the same named handler twice with different filters creates two subscriptions that call the same method, and a message matching both calls it twice; unsubscribe with that name removes both. When you want different filters for different work, use different handlers.

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
require 'smart_message'

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new
end

# messages/notice_message.rb
class NoticeMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  property :text, required: true
end

NoticeMessage.subscribe(broadcast: true)                 { |m| puts "broadcast   : #{m.text}" }
NoticeMessage.subscribe(to: 'billing')                   { |m| puts "to billing  : #{m.text}" }
NoticeMessage.subscribe(from: /\Aadmin-/)                { |m| puts "from admin  : #{m.text}" }
NoticeMessage.subscribe(to: 'billing', broadcast: true)  { |m| puts "billing+all : #{m.text}" }

NoticeMessage.new(text: 'one',   from: 'ops').publish                       # broadcast, billing+all
NoticeMessage.new(text: 'two',   from: 'ops', to: 'billing').publish        # to billing, billing+all
NoticeMessage.new(text: 'three', from: 'admin-1', to: 'shipping').publish   # from admin

SmartMessage.shutdown

docs.title: Inspecting subscriptions
docs.text:
transport = NoticeMessage.transport
transport.subscribers['NoticeMessage']
# => [{ subscriber_id: "NoticeMessage.proc_...", process_method: "...", filters: { broadcast: true, to: nil, from: nil } }, ...]

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text: A handler is the code that runs when a subscribed message arrives. You publish instances and subscribe at the class level.

docs.title: The default handler
docs.text:
MessageClass.subscribe with no argument subscribes the class method process:

# messages/order_message.rb
class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'order-service'
  property :order_id, required: true

  def self.process(message)
    Fulfillment.start(message.order_id)
  end
end

OrderMessage.subscribe   # handler id "OrderMessage.process"

A class that subscribes this way must define self.process (a class method). If it does not, subscribe raises ArgumentError.

docs.title: A named class method
docs.text:
Pass "ClassName.method_name". The method is looked up when a message arrives, so the class can be defined after the subscription. If the class is already defined, subscribe checks that it has that class method and raises ArgumentError if not. A handler that is not a "Class.method" String, a Proc or a block (a Symbol, for example), or whose class part can never name a class ("lower.handle", ".process", or a path through a constant that is not a class or module), also raises ArgumentError.

class OrderAudit
  def self.record(message)
    AuditLog.append(message.to_h)
  end
end

OrderMessage.subscribe('OrderAudit.record')   # handler id "OrderAudit.record"

docs.title: A block
docs.text:
handler_id = OrderMessage.subscribe do |message|
  Metrics.increment('orders')
end
# handler id like "OrderMessage.proc_3f9a1c0b7d2e4a68"

docs.title: A proc or lambda
docs.text:
notify = ->(message) { Notifier.order_placed(message.order_id) }
handler_id = OrderMessage.subscribe(notify)

Blocks, procs and lambdas are kept in a process-wide registry under a generated id. Each subscribe call registers a new handler, even when you pass the same proc twice.

Give subscribe one handler: a handler argument together with a block raises ArgumentError.

All forms accept the filters from:, to: and broadcast:.

docs.title: What a handler receives
docs.text:
One argument: the message. Every handler gets its own copy, with its own header and its own nested values, so a handler that changes its message does not affect any other handler.

def self.process(message)
  message.order_id               # properties
  message.from                   # addressing
  message.uuid                   # header uuid
  message._sm_header.published_at
end

With every shipped transport the message has been through JSON, so some types differ from what was published: a Time property arrives as a String, Symbols as Strings, nested Hash keys as Symbols. See Serializers.

The message is not validated before the handler is called.

docs.title: Where handlers run
docs.text:
On the dispatcher's thread pool, not on the thread that published or received the message. Consequences:

  • publish returns before handlers have run.
  • Handlers for one message, and handlers for different messages, can run at the same time. Shared state needs its own locking.
  • Messages are not guaranteed to be handled in the order they were published.
  • A program that exits right after publishing should call SmartMessage.shutdown to wait for its handlers.

See Dispatcher.

docs.title: When a handler fails
docs.text:
A handler that raises (any StandardError or ScriptError):

  • does not affect other handlers of the same message
  • has its copy of the message written to the dead letter queue with transport: "handler:<handler id>"
  • has its deduplication reservation released, so a redelivery or a replay is processed again
  • counts as a failure against its own circuit breaker

After repeated failures the handler's circuit opens. While it is open the handler is not called; each message it would have received goes to the dead letter queue.

Nothing is raised to the publisher: a handler failure is visible in the log (when logging is configured), in SmartMessage::Stats, and in the dead letter queue.

docs.title: Unsubscribing
docs.text:
OrderMessage.unsubscribe                       # the default handler, "OrderMessage.process"
OrderMessage.unsubscribe('OrderAudit.record')  # a named handler
OrderMessage.unsubscribe(handler_id)           # a block/proc/lambda, by the id subscribe returned
OrderMessage.unsubscribe!                      # every handler of this class

Passing the block/proc/lambda itself instead of its id raises ArgumentError. A message already handed to the thread pool still runs its handler after an unsubscribe.

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
require 'smart_message'
require 'tmpdir'

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new
  config.dlq_path  = File.join(Dir.mktmpdir, 'dead_letters.jsonl')
end

# messages/task_message.rb
class TaskMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'scheduler'
  property :name, required: true

  def self.process(message)
    puts "default handler: #{message.name}"
  end
end

class TaskAudit
  def self.record(message)
    puts "named handler: #{message.name}"
  end
end

TaskMessage.subscribe
TaskMessage.subscribe('TaskAudit.record')
block_id = TaskMessage.subscribe { |message| puts "block handler: #{message.name}" }
TaskMessage.subscribe(->(message) { raise "lambda handler cannot do #{message.name}" })

TaskMessage.new(name: 'backup').publish
SmartMessage.shutdown

dlq = SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.default
puts <<~REPORT
  block handler id:  #{block_id}
  processed:         #{SmartMessage::Stats.get('TaskMessage', 'TaskMessage.process', 'processed')}
  dead letters:      #{dlq.size}
  dead letter error: #{dlq.peek[:error]}
REPORT

Three handlers print their line; the fourth raises, and its message is in the dead letter queue.

docs.title: Properties and Validation
docs.text:
A message class declares its content with property. SmartMessage::Base is a Hashie::Dash, so the Hashie options (default:, from:, with:, transform_with:, and coerce_key) work, and SmartMessage adds required:, validate:, validation_message: and description:.

# messages/order_message.rb
class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  description 'A customer order'
  version 2
  from 'order-service'

  property :order_id,
           required: true,
           message: 'order_id is required',
           description: 'Unique order identifier'

  property :amount,
           required: true,
           validate: ->(value) { value.is_a?(Numeric) && value.positive? },
           validation_message: 'amount must be a positive number'

  property :currency,
           default: 'USD',
           validate: %w[USD EUR GBP],
           description: 'ISO 4217 currency code'

  property :note
end

docs.title: Property options
docs.text: Option Meaning required: true The property must not be nil when the message is validated. May also be a proc, evaluated on the instance, that returns true when the property is required: -> { kind == 'physical' }, or ->(message) { message.kind == 'physical' } to receive the message. A plain proc is always given the message as well, so proc { |m = nil| m.kind == 'physical' } works. Any other object that responds to call (a Method, a service object) runs in its own context and is called with the message, or with nothing when its call takes no argument. A condition that raises makes the property required. message: Error text when a required property is missing default: Value used when none is given. A proc is called to produce it. validate: A validator (see below) validation_message: Error text when the validator fails description: Documentation for the property from:, with:, transform_with: Hashie property translation

docs.title: Reading and writing
docs.text:
order = OrderMessage.new(order_id: 'ORD-1', amount: 10)

order.order_id          # => "ORD-1"
order[:order_id]        # => "ORD-1"
order['order_id']       # => "ORD-1"
order.note = 'gift'
order.fields            # => #<Set: {:order_id, :amount, :currency, :note}>
order.payload_hash      # => { order_id: "ORD-1", amount: 10, currency: "USD", note: "gift" }
order.to_h              # the same plus :_sm_header, a plain Hash of the header fields

new accepts keyword arguments or a Hash, with String or Symbol keys. Keys that are not declared properties are ignored. from, to and reply_to are addressing, not properties; they go into the header.

Values are deep-copied when the message is built, so a message never shares nested Hashes, Arrays or Strings with the caller. Nested Hashes keep the keys they were given: only the top level of a message accepts both Strings and Symbols.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Nothing is validated in new. Validation runs when you call one of these, and publish calls validate!:

order = OrderMessage.new(amount: -5)   # no error

order.valid?              # => false
order.validation_errors
# => [
#   { property: :order_id, value: nil, message: "order_id is required", source: "message" },
#   { property: :amount, value: -5, message: "amount must be a positive number", source: "message" }
# ]

order.validate!           # raises SmartMessage::Errors::ValidationError

validation_errors returns one Hash per failure. source is "message" for a property of the message, "header" for a header field (a missing from, for instance), or "version_mismatch".

SmartMessage::Errors::ValidationError#errors holds the same Array, and the exception message lists every failure:

begin
  order.publish
rescue SmartMessage::Errors::ValidationError => e
  e.message   # => "OrderMessage#order_id: order_id is required; OrderMessage#amount: amount must be a positive number"
  e.errors.map { |error| error[:property] }   # => [:order_id, :amount]
end

Validation covers three things:

  1. the message's own properties: required rules, then validators
  2. the header: uuid, message_class, published_at, publisher_pid, version and from are required
  3. the header version must equal the class version

A validator is skipped when the value is nil; whether nil is acceptable is the required: rule's business. A validator that raises counts as a failed validation.

A message that arrives from a transport is not validated before the handler is called. Call message.valid? in the handler if you need to.

docs.title: Validator types
docs.text:
validate: value Passes when Proc or lambda it returns a truthy value; it is evaluated on the message instance, so it can read other properties Symbol the instance method with that name returns a truthy value for the value Regexp it matches value.to_s Class or Module value.is_a?(TheClassOrModule), so Enumerable or Comparable work too Array or Set it includes the value Range it covers the value anything else it equals the value 
class ShipmentMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'warehouse'

  property :tracking, validate: /\A[A-Z]{2}\d{9}\z/
  property :weight,   validate: 0.1..500.0
  property :carrier,  validate: %w[ups fedex dhl]
  property :items,    validate: Array
  property :insured
  property :insured_value,
           required: -> { insured },                      # required only when insured
           validate: ->(value) { value <= 10_000 }
end

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text: Required rules, validators and descriptions are inherited. A subclass can add its own or override one of its parent's; it cannot change the parent.

docs.title: Reserved property names
docs.text:
The framework reads or defines some names on every message. Declaring a property with one of them raises SmartMessage::Errors::ReservedPropertyName when the class is defined:

  • from, to, reply_to, uuid
  • publish, transport, transports, config, logger
  • validate!, valid?, validation_errors
  • to_h, to_hash, message_header
  • any name starting with _sm_
class TransferMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  property :from   # raises SmartMessage::Errors::ReservedPropertyName:
                   #   TransferMessage: property name 'from' is reserved by SmartMessage
end

SmartMessage::Base.reserved_property_name?(:to)        # => true
SmartMessage::Base.reserved_property_name?(:_sm_id)    # => true
SmartMessage::Base::RESERVED_PROPERTY_NAMES            # the list

ReservedPropertyName is an ArgumentError.

docs.title: Coercion
docs.text:
coerce_key (from Hashie::Extensions::Coercion) converts a value when it is assigned, both in new and afterwards. Its main use is to restore a type that JSON cannot carry:

require 'time'

class EventMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'events'
  property :occurred_at
  coerce_key :occurred_at, ->(value) { value.is_a?(String) ? Time.parse(value) : value }
end

See Serializers for the list of type changes on a JSON round trip.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  version 2
end

OrderMessage.version                       # => 2
OrderMessage.new._sm_header.version        # => 2

The version is a positive Integer, default 1, inherited by subclasses. A message whose header version differs from its class version fails validation with a "version_mismatch" error. Because received messages are not validated automatically, a handler that must reject other versions calls message.validate! or compares message._sm_header.version itself.

docs.title: Descriptions
docs.text:
OrderMessage.description                        # => "A customer order"
OrderMessage.property_description(:order_id)    # => "Unique order identifier"
OrderMessage.property_descriptions              # => { order_id: "...", currency: "..." }
OrderMessage.described_properties               # => [:order_id, :currency]
OrderMessage.new.description                    # the class description

A class without a description gets "<ClassName> is a SmartMessage". Property descriptions are inherited; the class description is not.

docs.title: Pretty printing
docs.text:
order.pretty_print                        # properties only
order.pretty_print(include_header: true)  # header, then properties

pretty_print uses the amazing_print gem when it is installed and Ruby's pp otherwise.

docs.title: Ideas to Think About
docs.text:
None of the ideas on this page are implemented. The code blocks are sketches of APIs that do not exist in SmartMessage 0.1.0. For what the gem does today, see the rest of this documentation.

This document analyzes potential enhancements to SmartMessage based on a comparison between the current implementation and an idealized vision of intelligent messaging.

docs.title: Current State vs. Vision
docs.text: A description was provided that envisioned SmartMessage as an advanced, intelligent messaging system. While the current implementation is solid and well-designed, there are significant opportunities for enhancement to move toward that vision.

docs.title: What Currently Matches:
docs.text:
• Message abstraction from transport mechanisms - The gem does abstract messages from their delivery systems

  • Pluggable architecture - Transports and serializers are classes you can replace; four transports and a JSON serializer ship with the gem

  • Multiple messaging patterns - Can handle 1-to-1, 1-to-many scenarios through subscription patterns

  • Error handling - Handler isolation, per-handler circuit breakers, and a dead letter queue for every failure

docs.title: Major Enhancement Opportunities:
docs.text: The following features were described in the vision but are not currently implemented:

docs.title: 1. Autonomous Self-Publishing
docs.text:
Vision: Messages autonomously publish themselves based on predefined triggers Current: Messages require explicit .publish calls Potential Implementation: 

class SmartMessage::Base
  # Add trigger-based publishing
  def self.publish_on(event_type, condition = nil, &block)
    @auto_publish_triggers ||= []
    @auto_publish_triggers << {
      event: event_type,
      condition: condition || block,
      target: self
    }
  end

  # Monitor system events and auto-publish when triggered
  def self.check_triggers(event_data)
    @auto_publish_triggers&.each do |trigger|
      if trigger[:condition].call(event_data)
        new(event_data).publish
      end
    end
  end
end

# Usage example:
class OrderStatusUpdate < SmartMessage::Base
  property :order_id
  property :status

  # Automatically publish when order status changes
  publish_on(:order_status_changed) do |event|
    event[:status] == 'shipped'
  end
end

docs.title: 2. Dynamic Content Transformation
docs.text:
Vision: On-the-fly format conversion for different subscribers Current: One serializer per message class Potential Implementation: 

class SmartMessage::Dispatcher
  # Route with format transformation
  def route_with_transformation(message_header, message_payload)
    @subscribers[message_header.message_class].each do |processor|
      # Get subscriber's preferred format
      preferred_format = get_subscriber_format(processor)

      # Transform if needed
      if preferred_format != message_header.format
        transformed_payload = transform_format(
          message_payload,
          from: message_header.format,
          to: preferred_format
        )
        route_to_processor(processor, message_header, transformed_payload)
      else
        route_to_processor(processor, message_header, message_payload)
      end
    end
  end

  private

  def transform_format(payload, from:, to:)
    # Convert between formats (JSON -> XML, etc.)
    case [from, to]
    when ['json', 'xml']
      json_to_xml(payload)
    when ['xml', 'json']
      xml_to_json(payload)
    # Add more transformations as needed
    end
  end
end

docs.title: 3. Contextual Awareness and Routing Intelligence
docs.text:
Vision: Intelligent routing based on context and subscriber relevance Current: Simple class-name-based dispatch Potential Implementation: 

class SmartMessage::IntelligentDispatcher < SmartMessage::Dispatcher
  def initialize
    super
    @subscriber_profiles = {}
    @routing_intelligence = RoutingIntelligence.new
  end

  def subscribe_with_profile(message_class, processor, profile: {})
    super(message_class, processor)
    @subscriber_profiles[processor] = profile
  end

  def route(message_header, message_payload)
    # Analyze message content
    message_context = analyze_message_context(message_payload)

    # Find relevant subscribers based on context
    relevant_subscribers = find_relevant_subscribers(
      message_header.message_class,
      message_context
    )

    # Route only to relevant subscribers
    relevant_subscribers.each do |processor|
      route_to_processor(processor, message_header, message_payload)
    end
  end

  private

  def find_relevant_subscribers(message_class, context)
    candidates = @subscribers[message_class] || []

    candidates.select do |processor|
      profile = @subscriber_profiles[processor]
      @routing_intelligence.is_relevant?(context, profile)
    end
  end
end

# Usage:
dispatcher.subscribe_with_profile(
  "OrderMessage",
  "FulfillmentService.process",
  profile: {
    interests: ['physical_goods'],
    regions: ['US', 'CA'],
    order_value_min: 100
  }
)

docs.title: 4. Feedback Mechanisms
docs.text:
Vision: Collect feedback from subscribers for continuous improvement Current: No feedback system Potential Implementation: 

class SmartMessage::Base
  def self.process_with_feedback(message_header, message_payload)
    start_time = Time.now

    begin
      result = process_without_feedback(message_header, message_payload)

      # Collect success feedback
      SmartMessage::FeedbackCollector.record_success(
        processor: "#{self}.process",
        message_class: message_header.message_class,
        processing_time: Time.now - start_time,
        result_quality: evaluate_result_quality(result)
      )

      result
    rescue => e
      # Collect failure feedback
      SmartMessage::FeedbackCollector.record_failure(
        processor: "#{self}.process",
        message_class: message_header.message_class,
        error: e,
        processing_time: Time.now - start_time
      )
      raise
    end
  end

  alias_method :process_without_feedback, :process
  alias_method :process, :process_with_feedback
end

module SmartMessage::FeedbackCollector
  def self.record_success(processor:, message_class:, processing_time:, result_quality:)
    # Store feedback for analysis
    feedback_store.record({
      type: 'success',
      processor: processor,
      message_class: message_class,
      processing_time: processing_time,
      result_quality: result_quality,
      timestamp: Time.now
    })
  end

  def self.analyze_processor_performance(processor)
    # Analyze collected feedback to provide insights
    feedback_store.analyze(processor)
  end
end

docs.title: 5. Security Features
docs.text:
Vision: Built-in encryption and authentication Current: No security features Potential Implementation: 

class SmartMessage::SecureTransport < SmartMessage::Transport::Base
  def initialize(options = {})
    super
    @encryption_key = options[:encryption_key]
    @auth_provider = options[:auth_provider]
  end

  def publish(message_header, message_payload)
    # Authenticate sender
    unless @auth_provider.authenticate(message_header.publisher_pid)
      raise SmartMessage::Errors::AuthenticationFailed
    end

    # Encrypt payload
    encrypted_payload = encrypt_payload(message_payload)

    # Add security metadata to header
    secure_header = message_header.dup
    secure_header.encrypted = true
    secure_header.encryption_algorithm = 'AES-256-GCM'

    super(secure_header, encrypted_payload)
  end

  protected

  def receive(message_header, message_payload)
    # Decrypt if needed
    if message_header.encrypted
      decrypted_payload = decrypt_payload(message_payload)
      super(message_header, decrypted_payload)
    else
      super
    end
  end

  private

  def encrypt_payload(payload)
    # Implement encryption logic
  end

  def decrypt_payload(encrypted_payload)
    # Implement decryption logic
  end
end

docs.title: Current Strengths to Preserve
docs.text:
The existing SmartMessage implementation has several strengths that should be maintained:

  1. Simplicity - Easy to understand and use
  2. Solid Architecture - Well-designed plugin system and separation of concerns
  3. Thread Safety - Proper concurrent processing
  4. Flexibility - Support for custom transports and serializers
  5. Testing - Good test coverage and patterns

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
While the current SmartMessage implementation is solid and functional, there's significant potential to evolve it toward a more intelligent messaging system. The key is to implement these enhancements gradually while preserving the simplicity and reliability that make the current system valuable.

The vision of autonomous, context-aware messaging is achievable, but it requires careful planning to ensure that added intelligence doesn't compromise the system's core strengths of simplicity and reliability.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start by turning logging on. SmartMessage logs nothing unless a logger is configured.

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.logger    = STDERR
  config.log_level = :debug
end

Then look at the dead letter queue, where every failure ends up:

dlq = SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.default
dlq.file_path
dlq.statistics
dlq.inspect_messages(limit: 5)

docs.title: TransportNotConfigured
docs.text:
SmartMessage::Errors::TransportNotConfigured: OrderMessage has no transport configured. Set one in the class (transport SmartMessage::Transport.create(:memory)) or globally (SmartMessage.configure { |config| config.transport = ... })

There is no default transport. Set one on the class (transport ...), on a parent class, or globally (config.transport = ...). See Configuration.

If the transport is set globally, check that SmartMessage.configure runs before the first publish or subscribe, and that nothing called SmartMessage.reset_configuration! in between.

docs.title: ValidationError on publish, but new worked
docs.text:
new does not validate; publish does. Inspect the message:

message.valid?
message.validation_errors   # each has :property, :value, :message, :source

A source of "header" with property: :from means the message has no sender: set from on the class or pass from: to new.

The error message itself says so:

OrderMessage#from: From entity ID is required for message routing and replies (declare from 'service-name' in the class or pass from: to new)

docs.title: ReservedPropertyName when a class is loaded
docs.text: A property uses a name the framework owns (from, to, reply_to, uuid, transport, logger, to_h, and others, or a name starting with _sm_). Rename the property. The full list is in Properties and Validation.

docs.title: The handler never runs
docs.text:
Work through these in order.

  1. Did the program exit first? Handlers run on a thread pool. In a short script, call SmartMessage.shutdown before the end.
  2. Is the class subscribed on the transport the message arrives on? MessageClass.transport.subscribers shows the subscriptions. A subscription made before the transport was changed belongs to the old transport.
  3. Does the transport deliver at all? The stdout transport calls handlers only with loopback: true. The memory transport with auto_process: false delivers only on process_all.
  4. Do the filters match? A to: filter never matches a broadcast (to is nil); add broadcast: true if you want both. See Message Filtering.
  5. Was it a duplicate? With deduplication on, a UUID that the handler has already processed is skipped. Check SmartMessage::Stats.get('OrderMessage', 'OrderMessage.process', 'duplicate').
  6. Did the handler raise, or is its circuit open? Then the message is in the dead letter queue. Check dispatcher.circuit_breaker_stats.
  7. Redis: was the subscriber connected when the message was published? Redis pub/sub does not keep messages for subscribers that are not connected. Also check that publisher and subscriber use the same namespace:.
  8. File: is the reader starting at the end? By default a new subscription sees only lines written after it started. Use read_from_end: false to read existing lines.

docs.title: The handler runs, but a property has the wrong type
docs.text: The message went through JSON. A Time arrives as a String, a Symbol as a String, nested Hash keys as Symbols. Declare coerce_key for properties that need their type back. See Serializers.

docs.title: Messages cross between environments or test runs on Redis
docs.text: Redis pub/sub channels are global to the server. The db number does not separate them. Give each environment, and each test run, its own namespace:. See Redis Transport.

docs.title: TransportError from the Redis transport
docs.text:
• ... is disconnected: the transport was disconnected; call transport.connect.
  • Redis did not confirm the subscription to ... within 5s: the server is unreachable or slow. Check the url, and raise subscribe_timeout if needed.

docs.title: PublishError, or a result that is partial?
docs.text:
Every transport (or some of them) failed. error.result.failed or result.failed lists each failed transport with its exception. The message is in the dead letter queue once per failed transport.

BreakerMachines::CircuitOpenError as the error means that transport's circuit is open after repeated failures. It closes again by itself after the reset time, or call transport.reset_transport_circuits! once the cause is fixed. See Circuit Breakers.

docs.title: UnknownMessageClass or MessageClassMismatch in the log
docs.text: A payload named a class that is not a loaded SmartMessage::Base subclass in the receiving process, or arrived on a channel that belongs to another class. The payload is in the dead letter queue. Make sure the receiving process loads the message class (for instance, requires everything under messages/).

docs.title: Where is the dead letter queue file?
docs.text:
SmartMessage.configuration.dlq_path

By default $SMART_MESSAGE_DLQ_PATH, else $XDG_STATE_HOME/smart_message/dead_letters.jsonl, else ~/.local/state/smart_message/dead_letters.jsonl. It is no longer dead_letters.jsonl in the working directory. See Dead Letter Queue.

docs.title: No log file appears
docs.text: That is the default. Set config.logger; config.logger = :default writes to log/smart_message.log. See Logging.

docs.title: Shutdown takes several seconds
docs.text:
SmartMessage.shutdown (also run at exit) waits up to config.shutdown_timeout seconds (default 5) for running handlers. A handler that is blocked holds the process until the timeout, then is killed and its message dead-lettered. Lower the timeout, or fix the handler.

A Redis subscriber thread or a file poller is stopped with transport.disconnect, not by SmartMessage.shutdown.

docs.title: Handlers slow the publisher down
docs.text: When the dispatcher's queue is full, the delivering thread runs handlers itself. Raise config.dispatcher_max_threads or config.dispatcher_max_queue before creating transports, or make the handlers faster. See Dispatcher.

docs.title: Looking at what is going on
docs.text:
transport  = OrderMessage.transport
dispatcher = transport.dispatcher

transport.connected?
transport.subscribers
transport.transport_circuit_stats
dispatcher.status
dispatcher.circuit_breaker_stats
OrderMessage.ddq_stats
SmartMessage::Stats.stat

docs.title: Reporting a problem
docs.text: Open an issue at https://github.com/MadBomber/smart_message/issues with the SmartMessage version (SmartMessage::VERSION), the Ruby version, the transport and its options, and the smallest program that shows the problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The repository has runnable example programs, grouped by the transport they use. Each directory has its own README that lists the programs and says how to run them.

Directory What it shows Needs examples/memory/ Messaging patterns, handlers, filtering, addressing, deduplication, the dead letter queue, logging and configuration, all in one process Nothing examples/file/ The file transport: appending messages to a file and tailing it Nothing examples/redis/ The Redis pub/sub transport A Redis server examples/city_scenario/ Several programs (emergency dispatch, fire, police, health and others) exchanging messages over Redis A Redis server

Run an example from the repository root so that it uses the checked-out library:

bundle exec ruby -Ilib examples/memory/<program>.rb

The message classes of the city scenario are in its messages/ directory, which is the layout recommended for applications: one SmartMessage::Base subclass per file under messages/.

docs.title: Small patterns
docs.text: The programs below are complete. Each runs on its own with the memory transport.

docs.title: Request and reply
docs.text:
reply_to tells the receiver where to send its answer. The requester subscribes to replies addressed to it.

require 'smart_message'

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new
end

# messages/price_request.rb
class PriceRequest < SmartMessage::Base
  property :sku, required: true

  def self.process(message)
    PriceReply.new(sku: message.sku, cents: 1299, from: 'pricing', to: message.reply_to).publish
  end
end

# messages/price_reply.rb
class PriceReply < SmartMessage::Base
  property :sku,   required: true
  property :cents, required: true
end

PriceRequest.subscribe
PriceReply.subscribe(to: 'storefront') do |reply|
  puts "storefront: #{reply.sku} costs #{reply.cents} cents"
end

PriceRequest.new(sku: 'WIDGET-1', from: 'storefront', to: 'pricing', reply_to: 'storefront').publish

SmartMessage.shutdown

docs.title: Broadcast with several subscribers
docs.text:
require 'smart_message'

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new
end

# messages/user_signed_up.rb
class UserSignedUp < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'accounts'
  property :email, required: true
end

UserSignedUp.subscribe { |message| puts "mailer: welcome mail to #{message.email}" }
UserSignedUp.subscribe { |message| puts "metrics: signup counted" }
UserSignedUp.subscribe { |message| puts "audit: #{message.uuid} recorded" }

UserSignedUp.new(email: 'ann@example.com').publish

SmartMessage.shutdown

Each block is a separate handler with its own copy of the message.

docs.title: Testing a message class
docs.text:
With auto_process: false the memory transport stores what was published instead of delivering it, which is what a unit test usually wants.

require 'smart_message'

# messages/invoice_message.rb
class InvoiceMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'billing'
  property :number, required: true
  property :total,  validate: ->(value) { value >= 0 }
end

transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new(auto_process: false)
InvoiceMessage.transport(transport)

InvoiceMessage.new(number: 'INV-7', total: 250).publish

entry   = transport.all_messages.first
decoded = transport.decode_message(entry[:payload])

puts <<~REPORT
  stored:  #{transport.message_count}
  class:   #{entry[:message_class]}
  number:  #{decoded.number}
  invalid: #{InvoiceMessage.new(total: -1).validation_errors.map { |error| error[:property] }.inspect}
REPORT

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
SmartMessage requires Ruby 4.0 or newer.

# Gemfile
gem 'smart_message'

bundle install

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
Save this as quick_start.rb and run ruby quick_start.rb. It uses the memory transport, so it needs no external service.

require 'smart_message'

# In an application this class lives in messages/welcome_message.rb
class WelcomeMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  description 'Welcomes a new user'
  from 'signup-service'
  transport SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new

  property :user_name, required: true
  property :email,     required: true,
                       validate: /\A[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\z/,
                       validation_message: 'email must look like an address'
  property :plan,      default: 'free', validate: %w[free pro]

  # The default handler: a class method named process
  def self.process(message)
    puts "Welcome #{message.user_name} <#{message.email}> on the #{message.plan} plan"
  end
end

# Subscribe the default handler (WelcomeMessage.process)
WelcomeMessage.subscribe

# Publish a message.  publish validates first and returns a PublishResult.
result = WelcomeMessage.new(user_name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com').publish
puts "Published #{result.uuid}: success=#{result.success?}"

# An invalid message is not sent.
begin
  WelcomeMessage.new(user_name: 'Bob', email: 'not-an-address').publish
rescue SmartMessage::Errors::ValidationError => e
  puts "Not published: #{e.message}"
end

# Handlers run on a thread pool.  Wait for them before the program ends.
SmartMessage.shutdown

Output (the Welcome line comes from another thread, so its position can vary):

Published 6c5f0f0e-...: success=true
Welcome Alice <alice@example.com> on the free plan
Not published: WelcomeMessage#email: email must look like an address

The rest of this page explains each part.

docs.title: Message classes
docs.text:
A message class inherits from SmartMessage::Base. In an application, keep message classes in a messages/ directory, one class per file.

class WelcomeMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  description 'Welcomes a new user'   # optional
  version 1                           # optional, default 1

  property :user_name, required: true
  property :plan,      default: 'free'
end

property accepts required:, message:, default:, validate:, validation_message: and description:. See Properties and Validation.

docs.title: A transport is required
docs.text:
There is no default transport. A message class gets one in either of two ways:

# On the class (subclasses inherit it)
WelcomeMessage.transport SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new

# Globally, for every class that does not set its own
SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new
end

Publishing or subscribing with no transport raises SmartMessage::Errors::TransportNotConfigured.

Four transports ship with the gem: memory, stdout, file and Redis pub/sub. They differ in what they guarantee; read Transports before choosing one for production.

docs.title: A sender is required
docs.text:
Every message needs a from. Set a default on the class, or pass it when building the message:

class WelcomeMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'signup-service'
end

WelcomeMessage.new(user_name: 'Alice', email: 'a@example.com', from: 'admin-console')

A message with no from fails validation. to and reply_to are optional; see Addressing.

docs.title: Building and validating
docs.text:
new never raises for a missing or invalid property. Validation happens when you ask for it, and when you publish.

message = WelcomeMessage.new(user_name: 'Bob')   # email is missing: no error yet

message.valid?              # => false
message.validation_errors   # => [{ property: :email, value: nil, message: "...", source: "message" }]
message.validate!           # raises SmartMessage::Errors::ValidationError

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
result = message.publish

publish calls validate!, sends the message on every configured transport, and returns a SmartMessage::PublishResult. It raises SmartMessage::Errors::PublishError when every transport fails. See Publishing.

docs.title: Subscribing
docs.text:
You subscribe at the class level. A handler is a class method, a block, a proc or a lambda.

# 1. The default handler: WelcomeMessage.process
WelcomeMessage.subscribe

# 2. A class method somewhere else, named as "Class.method"
WelcomeMessage.subscribe('Mailer.send_welcome')

# 3. A block
WelcomeMessage.subscribe do |message|
  Metrics.increment('signups', plan: message.plan)
end

# 4. A proc or lambda
audit = ->(message) { AuditLog.record(message.to_h) }
WelcomeMessage.subscribe(audit)

subscribe returns a handler id. Pass it to unsubscribe to remove that handler; unsubscribe! removes every handler of the class.

Handlers run on a thread pool, each with its own copy of the message. A handler that raises does not affect the others; its copy of the message goes to the dead letter queue.

docs.title: Waiting for handlers
docs.text:
Because handlers run on other threads, a short script can reach its last line before they finish. SmartMessage.shutdown waits for them:

SmartMessage.shutdown               # waits config.shutdown_timeout seconds (default 5)
SmartMessage.shutdown(timeout: 30)  # or as long as you say

SmartMessage also registers SmartMessage.shutdown with at_exit, so handlers that are still running when the process ends get the configured timeout to finish. Calling it yourself makes the wait explicit and lets you check the return value (true when everything finished in time). Call it once, at the end: after a shutdown the thread pools are closed, and a handler for any later message runs on the thread that published or received it.

docs.title: A second program: filters and two handlers
docs.text:
require 'smart_message'

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new
end

# messages/alert_message.rb
class AlertMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'monitoring'

  property :level, required: true, validate: %w[info warning critical]
  property :text,  required: true

  def self.process(message)
    puts "[#{message.level}] #{message.text} (to: #{message.to || 'everyone'})"
  end
end

# Every alert
AlertMessage.subscribe

# Only alerts addressed to the on-call entity
AlertMessage.subscribe(to: 'on-call') do |message|
  puts "PAGE on-call: #{message.text}"
end

AlertMessage.new(level: 'info', text: 'Deploy finished').publish
AlertMessage.new(level: 'critical', text: 'Database is down', to: 'on-call').publish

SmartMessage.shutdown

It prints three lines: both alerts from AlertMessage.process, and the page for the second one.

docs.title: Upgrading from 0.0.x
docs.text:
SmartMessage 0.1.0 is a reliability release that changes the public API in several places. This page walks through each breaking change in the CHANGELOG, with the code you had and the code you need.

A quick checklist:

  1. Run on Ruby 4.0 or newer.
  2. Give every message class a transport.
  3. Stop using the return value of publish as a number.
  4. Move validation rescues from new to publish / validate!.
  5. Rename any property that uses a reserved name.
  6. Configure a logger if you relied on the default log file.
  7. Decide where the dead letter queue file should live.
  8. Replace removed file transport and stdout transport options.
  9. Replace db: isolation of Redis environments with namespace:.

docs.title: Ruby 4.0
docs.text: The gem now requires Ruby 4.0 or newer (required_ruby_version = '>= 4.0').

docs.title: No default transport
docs.text:
Before, a message class with no transport fell back to a Redis connection on localhost. Now there is no fallback.

# Before: published to Redis on localhost without being told to
class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  property :order_id
end
OrderMessage.new(order_id: 1, from: 'orders').publish

# After: say which transport
class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  transport SmartMessage::Transport.create(:redis, namespace: 'production')
  property :order_id
end

# or once, for every class without its own
SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport.create(:redis, namespace: 'production')
end

Publishing or subscribing without a transport raises SmartMessage::Errors::TransportNotConfigured.

docs.title: publish returns a PublishResult
docs.text:
Before, publish returned a running count of published messages, and a transport that failed could still be counted as a success. Now it returns a SmartMessage::PublishResult with one outcome per transport.

# Before
count = message.publish

# After
result = message.publish
result.success?     # every transport accepted it
result.partial?     # some accepted it, some failed
result.failure?     # none accepted it (publish raises in this case)
result.successful   # Array of outcomes
result.failed       # Array of outcomes; outcome.error is the exception
result.errors       # the exceptions
result.outcomes     # every outcome

When every transport fails, publish raises SmartMessage::Errors::PublishError, and the result is on error.result:

begin
  message.publish
rescue SmartMessage::Errors::PublishError => e
  e.result.failed.each { |outcome| warn "#{outcome.transport_name}: #{outcome.error.message}" }
end

Transport#publish (the method on a transport instance) now raises the transport's own error. It used to return a fallback Hash when its circuit breaker tripped.

If you need the count, read it from SmartMessage::Stats.get('OrderMessage', 'publish').

See Publishing.

docs.title: Validation happens in one place
docs.text:
Before, new raised for a missing required property or a missing from. Now new never validates.

# Before
OrderMessage.new(amount: 5)            # raised: order_id is required

# After
message = OrderMessage.new(amount: 5)  # no error
message.valid?                         # => false
message.validation_errors              # => [{ property: :order_id, value: nil, message: "...", source: "message" }]

begin
  message.publish                      # publish calls validate!
rescue SmartMessage::Errors::ValidationError => e
  e.errors                             # the same Array that validation_errors returns
end

Code that built a message and assumed it was valid because new returned should call valid? or validate!.

See Properties and Validation.

docs.title: Reserved property names
docs.text:
Declaring a property with one of these names raises SmartMessage::Errors::ReservedPropertyName when the class is defined:

from, to, reply_to, uuid, publish, transport, transports, config, logger, validate!, valid?, validation_errors, to_h, to_hash, message_header, and anything starting with _sm_.

# Before: accepted, and collided with the framework at run time
class TransferMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  property :from
  property :to
end

# After: choose names that say what the values are
class TransferMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  property :source_account
  property :target_account
end

docs.title: Message hashes
docs.text:
Nested Hashes keep the keys they were given. Before, they were converted to indifferent-access hashes; now only the top level of a message accepts both Strings and Symbols.

message = OrderMessage.new(order_id: 1, customer: { 'name' => 'Ann' })

# Before
message.customer[:name]     # => "Ann"

# After
message.customer['name']    # => "Ann"
message.customer[:name]     # => nil

After a JSON round trip (that is, in a handler), nested keys are Symbols. See Serializers.

to_h returns the header as a plain Hash under :_sm_header, not a SmartMessage::Header object:

message.to_h[:_sm_header]          # => { uuid: "...", message_class: "OrderMessage", ... }
message.to_h[:_sm_header][:uuid]   # After
message._sm_header.uuid            # the Header object is still here

docs.title: Class settings are inherited the same way everywhere
docs.text:
Transport, logger, version, addressing, deduplication settings, validators and property descriptions are read from the class, else from its parent. A subclass can no longer change its parent or a sibling.

class BaseEvent < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'events'
  transport SmartMessage::Transport.create(:memory)
end

class UserEvent < BaseEvent
  from 'user-service'    # changes UserEvent only
end

BaseEvent.from   # => "events"   (before: could become "user-service")
UserEvent.transport.equal?(BaseEvent.transport)   # => true, inherited

description is the exception: it is not inherited. A subclass without its own description gets the default "<ClassName> is a SmartMessage".

docs.title: Logging is off unless configured
docs.text:
Before, SmartMessage created log/smart_message.log and wrote to it by default. Now nothing is logged and no directory is created unless you configure a logger.

# To get the 0.0.x behaviour back
SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.logger = :default   # Lumberjack logger writing to log/smart_message.log
end

The three shipped loggers (Lumberjack, Default, Null) now share one interface, SmartMessage::Logger::Base. In the Lumberjack JSON format, keyword data given to a log call is nested under "data":

logger.info('Order placed', order_id: 42)
# Before: order_id was a top-level field of the JSON line
# After:  {"timestamp":"...","level":"INFO","message":"Order placed","source":"...","data":{"order_id":42}}

See Logging.

docs.title: Dead letter queue location
docs.text:
Before, the default dead letter queue was dead_letters.jsonl in the current working directory. Now it is, in order:

  1. $SMART_MESSAGE_DLQ_PATH, when set
  2. $XDG_STATE_HOME/smart_message/dead_letters.jsonl, when XDG_STATE_HOME is set
  3. ~/.local/state/smart_message/dead_letters.jsonl
# To choose the file
SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.dlq_path = '/var/lib/my_app/dead_letters.jsonl'
end

If you have an old dead_letters.jsonl with entries you still need, point config.dlq_path at it or create a queue for it with SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.new('dead_letters.jsonl') and replay from there.

See Dead Letter Queue.

docs.title: Deduplication API
docs.text:
Deduplication queues now belong to the dispatcher: one per handler per message class. The dispatcher reserves a UUID before the handler runs and releases it if the handler fails, so you no longer mark messages yourself.

# Before
def self.process(message)
  return if message.duplicate?
  handle(message)
  message.mark_as_processed!
end

# After: the dispatcher has already done it
def self.process(message)
  handle(message)
end

Removed: message.duplicate?, message.mark_as_processed!, MessageClass.duplicate_uuid?, MessageClass.get_ddq_instance.

ddq_stats has a new shape:

OrderMessage.ddq_stats
# Before: one flat Hash for the class
# After:
# {
#   enabled: true,
#   queues: {
#     "OrderMessage:OrderMessage.process" => { size: 100, storage_type: :memory, current_count: 3, ... }
#   }
# }

The Redis backend stores one key per UUID with a TTL instead of a list and a set. ddq_size no longer bounds Redis storage; use the ttl: option:

ddq_storage :redis, ttl: 3600   # seconds; 3600 is the default

Custom backends must implement atomic reserve(uuid) and release(uuid).

See Message Deduplication.

docs.title: Circuit breakers
docs.text:
• There is one circuit per transport instance and one per handler per message class. A failing handler no longer opens the circuit for other handlers.
  • Each circuit keeps its state in memory. The storage: :redis option is gone.
  • SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker::Fallbacks procs take the error only.
  • Serializers are no longer wrapped in a circuit. A failed encode raises SmartMessage::Errors::SerializationError; a failed decode raises SmartMessage::Errors::DecodeError.
# Before
SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker::Fallbacks.dead_letter_queue        # proc { |exception, *args| ... }

# After: the message comes from a block evaluated on the circuit's owner
SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker::Fallbacks.dead_letter_queue { current_message }   # proc { |exception| ... }

For retries, use the new SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker.with_retries loop. See Circuit Breakers.

docs.title: File transport
docs.text:
The file transport is now an append-only JSON Lines writer with a tailing poller. Named pipe support, the asynchronous publish queue, file rotation and partitioned files are removed, along with their options (file_type, async, rotate_size, directory, subscription_mode, and the rest). file_path: is required.

# Before
SmartMessage::Transport::FileTransport.new(
  file_path: 'messages.log', file_format: :lines, async: true, rotate_size: 10_000_000
)

# After: the only options
SmartMessage::Transport::FileTransport.new(
  file_path:          'messages.jsonl',   # required
  create_directories: true,
  encoding:           nil,
  poll_interval:      0.5,
  read_from_end:      true
)

If you need rotation, rotate the file with an external tool; a reader starts again from the beginning when the file becomes shorter than what it has consumed. See File Transport.

docs.title: Stdout transport
docs.text:
StdoutTransport no longer inherits from the file transport. Its options are output: (an IO) and loopback:. It never closes the IO; before, disconnect closed $stdout.

# Before
SmartMessage::Transport::StdoutTransport.new(file_path: 'messages.log')

# After
SmartMessage::Transport::StdoutTransport.new                    # writes to $stdout
SmartMessage::Transport::StdoutTransport.new(output: $stderr)
SmartMessage::Transport::FileTransport.new(file_path: 'messages.jsonl')   # to write to a file

See Stdout Transport.

docs.title: Memory transport
docs.text:
• Stored entries are { message_class:, payload:, published_at: }. The payload is the serialized String (before: a message: key holding the message object).
  • Messages are stored only when auto_process: false, or when you pass store_messages: true. Before, every message was stored.
  • process_all removes what it delivers, so calling it twice does not deliver twice.
  • Messages are serialized and decoded on delivery, as a real transport does. Handlers therefore see JSON type changes (a Time property arrives as a String). Pass serialize: false to hand handlers copies of the published object instead.
# Before
transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new
message.publish
transport.all_messages.first[:message].order_id

# After
transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new(store_messages: true)
message.publish
entry = transport.all_messages.first
transport.decode_message(entry[:payload]).order_id

See Memory Transport.

docs.title: Redis transport
docs.text:
• Publishing or subscribing after disconnect raises SmartMessage::Errors::TransportError until you call connect.
  • subscribe returns once Redis has confirmed the subscription, or raises TransportError after subscribe_timeout seconds (default 5).
  • New namespace: option. Redis pub/sub channels are global to the server; the db number never separated them.
# Before: did not isolate anything for pub/sub
SmartMessage::Transport::RedisTransport.new(url: 'redis://localhost:6379', db: 15)

# After
SmartMessage::Transport::RedisTransport.new(url: 'redis://localhost:6379', namespace: 'test')

See Redis Transport.

docs.title: Transport.create
docs.text:
# Before
SmartMessage::Transport.create(:nope)   # => nil

# After
SmartMessage::Transport.create(:nope)   # raises ArgumentError: Unknown transport: :nope. Available: [:memory, :stdout, :file, :redis]

docs.title: Removed
