docs.text: Removed Use instead SimpleStats SmartMessage::Stats (add, get, reset, stat) SmartMessage::Base.decode transport.decode_message(payload) or SmartMessage::Envelope.decode(payload, serializer:) SmartMessage::Errors::SerializerNotConfigured Not raised any more; a transport always has a serializer The _version accessor MessageClass.version, message._sm_header.version Dependencies on activesupport, async, async-redis, colorize Add them to your own Gemfile if your code used them through SmartMessage

docs.title: MessageClass.header takes a block only
docs.text:
# Still works
class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  header do
    from 'order-service'
    to   'fulfillment'
  end
end

# Raises ArgumentError
OrderMessage.header          # no block
OrderMessage.header(:from)   # arguments

To read a message's header, use message._sm_header (or message.message_header).

docs.title: Extension transport gems
docs.text: The separate smart_message-transport-* gems (NATS, RabbitMQ, named pipes, lanet) have not yet been updated for 0.1.0.

docs.title: Circuit Breakers
docs.text:
A circuit breaker stops calling something that keeps failing. SmartMessage builds its circuits on the BreakerMachines gem and keeps two kinds:

Circuit Scope Default threshold Default reset Transport publish one per transport instance 5 failures within 30 seconds try again after 15 seconds Message processor one per handler per message class 3 failures within 60 seconds try again after 30 seconds

Every circuit has its own in-memory state. A failure in one never opens another: a handler that fails does not stop other handlers, and one transport's failures do not stop another transport.

A circuit is closed (calls go through), open (calls are rejected without being made), or half-open (after the reset time, a trial call decides whether it closes again).

docs.title: The transport circuit
docs.text:
transport.publish runs the actual send inside the transport's circuit.

  • A failing send raises its own error.
  • Once the threshold is reached the circuit opens, and further publishes on that transport raise BreakerMachines::CircuitOpenError without contacting the medium.

Through message.publish both cases are recorded as that transport's failed outcome in the PublishResult and the message is written to the dead letter queue.

transport.transport_circuit_stats
# => { transport_publish: { status: :closed, closed: true, open: false, half_open: false, last_error: nil, stats: {...} } }

transport.reset_transport_circuits!   # close it and forget its failures

docs.title: The handler circuits
docs.text:
The dispatcher runs each handler inside the circuit for that handler and message class, named "<MessageClass>:<handler id>".

  • A handler that raises counts as a failure, and its message goes to the dead letter queue.
  • While the circuit is open the handler is not called. Each message it would have received goes to the dead letter queue with a BreakerMachines::CircuitOpenError, and any deduplication reservation is released, so those messages can be replayed once the cause is fixed.
dispatcher = OrderMessage.transport.dispatcher

dispatcher.circuit_breaker_stats
# => { "OrderMessage:OrderMessage.process" => { status: :open, closed: false, open: true, half_open: false, last_error: #<RuntimeError ...>, stats: {...} } }

dispatcher.reset_circuit_breakers!('OrderMessage:OrderMessage.process')   # one circuit
dispatcher.reset_circuit_breakers!                                        # all of them

A circuit is created the first time its handler runs and discarded when the handler is unsubscribed.

docs.title: Circuit events in the log
docs.text:
When a circuit opens, closes, or half-opens, BreakerMachines reports it with a line such as [BreakerMachines] Circuit 'OrderMessage:OrderMessage.process' opened. SmartMessage sends those lines to its own logger: opening is logged at warn, the others at info. With no logger configured nothing is written.

If your application gives BreakerMachines a logger of its own (BreakerMachines.logger = ...) before it loads SmartMessage's circuit breakers, that logger is kept. To drop the events altogether:

require 'breaker_machines'

BreakerMachines.configure { |config| config.log_events = false }

docs.title: Changing the thresholds
docs.text:
Pass circuit_breaker: when you create a transport. Give only the values you want to change:

transport = SmartMessage::Transport.create(
  :redis,
  namespace: 'production',
  circuit_breaker: {
    transport_publish: { threshold: { failures: 10, within: 60 }, reset_after: 30 },
    message_processor: { threshold: { failures: 5 } }
  }
)

message_processor applies to every handler circuit of that transport's dispatcher. If you build the dispatcher yourself, pass the options to it: SmartMessage::Dispatcher.new({ message_processor: { reset_after: 10 } }).

The defaults are in SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker::DEFAULT_CONFIGS.

docs.title: Retries: with_retries
docs.text:
SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker.with_retries is a bounded retry loop with exponential backoff. It is independent of the circuits; use it around a call that may fail transiently.

result = SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker.with_retries(max_retries: 3, base_delay: 0.5, max_delay: 10) do |attempt|
  message.publish
end
Option Default Meaning max_retries 3 Retries after the first attempt base_delay 1 Seconds before the first retry; doubles each time max_delay 30 Upper bound for one delay on [StandardError] Exception classes worth retrying sleeper Kernel.method(:sleep) How to wait; replace it in tests

The block receives the attempt number, starting at 0. The block's value is returned. When every attempt fails, the last error is raised.

Put with_retries around a circuit-protected call, not inside one, so that each attempt counts against the circuit. Limit on: to errors that can succeed on a retry; retrying a ValidationError is pointless:

SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker.with_retries(on: [SmartMessage::Errors::PublishError]) { message.publish }

Note that every failed attempt of message.publish writes a dead letter queue entry.

docs.title: Using circuits in your own code
docs.text:
Build a standalone circuit:

circuit = SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker.build(
  'inventory-api',
  { threshold: { failures: 3, within: 60 }, reset_after: 30 }
)

circuit.wrap { InventoryApi.reserve(sku) }   # raises the block's error, or BreakerMachines::CircuitOpenError

SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker.available?(circuit)   # => false while it is open
SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker.stats(circuit)        # => { name:, state:, failure_count:, success_count:, last_failure_at:, opened_at:, last_error: }
SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker.reset!(circuit)

A circuit built this way has no fallback: the caller decides what to do with the error.

For a class that uses the BreakerMachines DSL (circuit(:name).wrap { ... }), SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker.configure_for(klass) adds the two default circuits, and SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker::Fallbacks provides fallback procs. A fallback proc receives the error only and is evaluated on the object that owns the circuit:

class PaymentService
  include BreakerMachines::DSL

  attr_accessor :current_message

  circuit :gateway do
    threshold failures: 3, within: 60
    reset_after 30
    fallback SmartMessage::CircuitBreaker::Fallbacks.dead_letter_queue { current_message }
  end

  def charge(message)
    self.current_message = message
    circuit(:gateway).wrap { Gateway.charge(message.amount) }
  end
end

Fallbacks.dead_letter_queue(dlq = nil) { message } stores the message in the dead letter queue and returns { circuit_breaker: { state:, rejected:, error:, error_class:, timestamp:, sent_to_dlq: } }. Fallbacks.graceful_degradation(response) returns the same shape with degraded_response:.

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
require 'smart_message'
require 'tmpdir'

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.dlq_path = File.join(Dir.mktmpdir, 'dead_letters.jsonl')
end

transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new(
  circuit_breaker: { message_processor: { threshold: { failures: 2, within: 60 }, reset_after: 30 } }
)

# messages/sync_message.rb
class SyncMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'sync'
  property :n

  @calls = 0

  class << self
    attr_accessor :calls

    def process(_message)
      self.calls += 1
      raise 'remote system is down'
    end
  end
end

SyncMessage.transport(transport)
SyncMessage.subscribe

5.times do |n|
  SyncMessage.new(n: n).publish
  sleep 0.05 until transport.dispatcher.status[:in_flight].zero?
end
SmartMessage.shutdown

circuit = transport.dispatcher.circuit_breaker_stats['SyncMessage:SyncMessage.process']
errors  = SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.default.entries.map { |entry| entry[:error][/\A[\w:]+/] }.tally

puts <<~REPORT
  handler calls: #{SyncMessage.calls}
  circuit open:  #{circuit[:open]}
  dead letters:  #{errors}
REPORT

The handler is called twice. The circuit then opens, and the remaining three messages go to the dead letter queue without the handler being called. The output also has the BreakerMachines line announcing that the circuit opened.

docs.title: Dead Letter Queue
docs.text: The dead letter queue (DLQ) is a file that holds messages SmartMessage could not publish or process. It uses the JSON Lines format: one JSON object per line, oldest first. Entries can be inspected, filtered and replayed.

docs.title: Where the file is
docs.text:
The default queue uses the first of these that applies:

  1. config.dlq_path, when you set it
  2. the environment variable SMART_MESSAGE_DLQ_PATH
  3. $XDG_STATE_HOME/smart_message/dead_letters.jsonl, when XDG_STATE_HOME is set
  4. ~/.local/state/smart_message/dead_letters.jsonl
SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.dlq_path = '/var/lib/my_app/dead_letters.jsonl'
end

SmartMessage.configuration.dlq_path    # => "/var/lib/my_app/dead_letters.jsonl"
SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.default  # the queue at that path

The path is always stored as an absolute path, so it never depends on the working directory. The directory is created when the queue is first used. A sidecar file <path>.lock appears next to the queue file; it is the lock described below.

SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.configure_default(path) is a shortcut that sets config.dlq_path and returns the queue.

You can also work with any queue file directly:

queue = SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.new('/tmp/payments_dlq.jsonl')

docs.title: What lands in it
docs.text:
SmartMessage writes to the default queue in five situations:

Situation transport field of the entry error field A transport failed to publish the message the transport's class name the transport's error A received payload could not be decoded (not an envelope, unknown message class, class does not match the channel) the transport's class name the decode error A handler raised handler:<handler id> the handler's error A handler's circuit breaker was open, so the handler was not called handler:<handler id> BreakerMachines::CircuitOpenError: ... A handler was still running when the shutdown timeout expired and was killed handler:<handler id> SmartMessage::Errors::Error: Dispatcher shut down before the handler finished

A publish that fails on several transports writes one entry per failed transport. A message with several handlers writes one entry per failed handler.

If writing to the queue itself fails, that is logged at error level and the original error is still raised or recorded.

docs.title: Entry format
docs.text:
{
  "id": "8a4c3c53-5d1b-4d0c-9a57-3e0b7c6f4d11",
  "timestamp": "2026-11-11T10:15:30.123-06:00",
  "header": { "uuid": "0b0e6f0c-...", "message_class": "OrderMessage", "published_at": "2026-11-11T10:15:30.123456-06:00", "publisher_pid": 4242, "version": 1, "from": "order-service", "serializer": "SmartMessage::Serializer::Json" },
  "payload": "{\"_sm_header\":{...},\"order_id\":\"ORD-1\"}",
  "payload_format": "json",
  "error": "RuntimeError: inventory service is down",
  "retry_count": 0,
  "transport": "handler:OrderMessage.process",
  "stack_trace": "..."
}
Field Meaning id Unique id of the entry timestamp When the entry was written header The message header, for reading and filtering. For a payload that could not be decoded, only message_class (the channel it arrived for, or "Unknown"). Replay uses the header inside payload, and fails when that header names a different class than this message_class (unless it is "Unknown"). payload The serialized message, including its header payload_format Serializer of the payload: "json", or the serializer class name for a payload a transport with another serializer could not receive error "ErrorClass: message" retry_count Number of failed replays transport Where it failed (see the table above) stack_trace Backtrace, when there was one

Methods that return entries return Hashes with Symbol keys.

docs.title: Inspecting
docs.text:
dlq = SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.default

dlq.size                        # number of lines in the file
dlq.empty?
dlq.peek                        # oldest entry, not removed
dlq.entries                     # every valid entry, oldest first
dlq.inspect_messages(limit: 10) # the first 10 entries

dlq.filter_by_class('OrderMessage')
dlq.filter_by_error_pattern(/timeout/i)       # a Regexp or a String
dlq.export_range(Time.now - 3600, Time.now)   # by entry timestamp

dlq.statistics
# => { total: 3, by_class: { "OrderMessage" => 3 }, by_error: { "RuntimeError: ..." => 3 }, corrupt: 0 }

docs.title: Replaying
docs.text:
Replay rebuilds the message from the entry, with its original header and the same UUID, and publishes it again.

dlq.replay_one                # the oldest entry
dlq.replay_batch(10)          # the oldest 10
dlq.replay_all                # everything in the queue right now

dlq.replay_one(transport)     # each takes an optional transport to publish on instead
dlq.replay_batch(10, transport)
dlq.replay_all(transport)

replay_one returns { success: true, message: } or { success: false, error: }. replay_batch and replay_all return { success: <count>, failed: <count>, errors: [...] }.

Replay semantics:

  • Replay publishes; it does not call a handler. The message goes out on its class's transports (or the override) and reaches whoever is subscribed, like any published message. This is true for handler failures too: replaying an entry whose transport is handler:OrderMessage.process republishes the message, and every current subscriber of the class receives it, not only the handler that failed. Enable deduplication if the other handlers must not process it again; the failed handler's reservation was released, so it will run.
  • An entry is removed only after it has been published again. A replay that fails leaves the entry in the queue, with retry_count raised by one and error replaced by "Replay failed: ...".
  • The message class must be loaded. Replay needs the SmartMessage::Base subclass named in the entry, and that class needs a transport (or pass one).
  • The message is validated again before it is sent. An invalid message counts as a failed replay.
  • An undecodable payload cannot be replayed as it is. Its replay fails for the same reason it could not be decoded, and it stays in the queue for inspection.
  • A failed replay does not add a second entry. Replay sends straight to the transports, not through publish, so a transport failure only updates the existing entry. Transports are tried in order and replay stops at the first failure, so any before the failing one have already sent the message, and the next replay sends it to them again.

dequeue removes and returns the oldest entry without publishing it. clear deletes the queue file.

docs.title: Adding entries yourself
docs.text:
dlq.enqueue(message, error: 'Rejected by the fraud check', transport: 'manual')

dlq.enqueue_raw(
  message_class: 'OrderMessage',
  payload:       raw_string,
  error_info:    { error: 'Could not parse', transport: 'import-script' }
)

enqueue accepts :error, :retry_count, :transport and :stack_trace. enqueue_raw stores a payload untouched, for bytes that could not be turned into a message; its error_info also accepts :serializer.

docs.title: Concurrency and durability
docs.text:
• Every read-modify-write runs under an exclusive lock on <file>.lock, so several threads and several processes can share one queue file.
  • Appends are flushed to disk (fsync).
  • Rewrites (after dequeue or a replay) go to a temporary file that is then renamed over the queue, so a crash does not leave a half-written queue.
  • A corrupt line does not stop later lines from being read. statistics[:corrupt] counts corrupt lines; dequeue drops the corrupt lines ahead of the entry it returns and logs a warning.

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
require 'smart_message'
require 'tmpdir'

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new
  config.dlq_path  = File.join(Dir.mktmpdir, 'dead_letters.jsonl')
end

# messages/payment_message.rb
class PaymentMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'checkout'
  property :amount, required: true

  @gateway_up = false

  class << self
    attr_accessor :gateway_up

    def process(message)
      raise 'payment gateway is down' unless gateway_up

      puts "charged #{message.amount}"
    end
  end
end

PaymentMessage.subscribe
PaymentMessage.new(amount: 25).publish

dispatcher = PaymentMessage.transport.dispatcher
sleep 0.05 until dispatcher.status[:in_flight].zero?   # wait for the handler to fail

dlq   = SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.default
entry = dlq.peek
puts <<~REPORT
  queue file: #{dlq.file_path}
  entries:    #{dlq.size}
  error:      #{entry[:error]}
  failed in:  #{entry[:transport]}
REPORT

# Fix the problem, then replay
PaymentMessage.gateway_up = true
outcome = dlq.replay_one

SmartMessage.shutdown
puts "replayed: #{outcome[:success]}, entries left: #{dlq.size}"

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Logging is off unless you configure it. With no logger configured, SmartMessage writes nothing and creates no file or directory.

docs.title: config.logger
docs.text:
SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.logger = 'log/my_app.log'
end
Value Result nil No logging. This is the default. :default The built-in Lumberjack logger writing to log/smart_message.log (under Rails.root in a Rails application) a String or Pathname path The built-in Lumberjack logger writing to that file. The directory is created. STDOUT or STDERR The built-in Lumberjack logger writing to the console a logger object Used as it is: Rails.logger, Logger.new(...), a SmartMessage::Logger::Default, or your own. It must respond to debug, info, warn, error and fatal; anything else raises ArgumentError when assigned

Any object with the standard Ruby Logger interface works. The framework only calls debug, info, warn, error and fatal, each with a block.

docs.title: The log_* settings
docs.text:
These shape the built-in Lumberjack logger, that is, when config.logger is :default, a String path, STDOUT or STDERR. They have no effect on a logger object you supply.

Setting Values Default config.log_level :debug, :info, :warn, :error, :fatal :info config.log_format :text or :json :text config.log_include_source true / false: add file:line of the caller true config.log_structured_data true / false: keep keyword data given to log calls true config.log_colorize true / false: colour lines by level; console output only false config.log_options a Hash of rotation options (below) {}

log_level and log_format also accept Strings ('warn', 'json'). Any other value raises ArgumentError when it is assigned.

Rotation options for config.log_options:

Key Meaning roll_by_size: true Rotate by size max_file_size: Bytes per file when rotating by size (default 10 MB) keep_files: Files to keep when rotating by size (default 5) roll_by_date: true Rotate by date roll_period: 'daily' (default), 'weekly' or 'monthly' date_pattern: Suffix pattern for rotated files, such as '%Y-%m-%d' 
SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.logger              = 'log/smart_message.log'
  config.log_level           = :debug
  config.log_format          = :json
  config.log_include_source  = true
  config.log_structured_data = true
  config.log_options         = { roll_by_size: true, max_file_size: 50 * 1024 * 1024, keep_files: 10 }
end

The logger is built once, when it is first needed, and rebuilt only after one of these settings changes.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Text format:

[2026-11-11 10:15:30.123] INFO  -- messaging.rb:77 : [SmartMessage] Published: OrderMessage via MemoryTransport

JSON format, one object per line. Keyword data given to a log call is nested under data, so it cannot collide with the fixed fields:

{"timestamp":"2026-11-11 10:15:30.123","level":"INFO","message":"Order accepted","source":"orders.rb:12","data":{"order_id":42}}

The circuit breakers (the BreakerMachines gem) report through the same logger: a circuit opening is logged at warn, closing and half-opening at info. See Circuit Breakers.

docs.title: What SmartMessage logs
docs.text: Level Events debug Message created, routing decisions, subscriptions added, skipped Redis payloads info Published (with the transports used), subscribed, unsubscribed warn Partial publish failure, duplicate skipped, corrupt dead letter queue lines dropped error Transport publish failure, handler failure, payload that cannot be received, lost Redis subscriber connection, handler killed at shutdown, dead letter queue write failure

docs.title: Using the logger yourself
docs.text:
logger = SmartMessage::Logger.default   # the configured logger, or a Null logger

logger.info('Order accepted')
logger.info { "built only when the level allows it" }
logger.info('Order accepted', order_id: 42)   # keyword data
logger.level = :debug                          # Symbol, String or Integer
logger.debug?                                  # => true
logger.add(:warn, 'text')

Keyword data, level= with a Symbol and add with a Symbol belong to the interface of the loggers shipped with SmartMessage (SmartMessage::Logger::Base). A plain Ruby Logger does not accept keyword data.

docs.title: The shipped loggers
docs.text: All three inherit from SmartMessage::Logger::Base and share one interface.

docs.title: SmartMessage::Logger::Lumberjack
docs.text:
What config.logger = :default, a path, STDOUT or STDERR builds. You can also build one yourself:

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.logger = SmartMessage::Logger::Lumberjack.new(
    log_file:        STDERR,   # a path, STDOUT or STDERR
    level:           :debug,
    format:          :text,    # :text or :json
    include_source:  true,
    structured_data: true,
    colorize:        true      # console only
  )
end

docs.title: SmartMessage::Logger::Default
docs.text:
A thin wrapper around Ruby's standard Logger. Each line carries the caller's file and line.

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.logger = SmartMessage::Logger::Default.new(
    log_file: 'log/smart_message.log',   # a path or an IO; this path is the default
    level:    :info                      # default :info
  )
end

Given a path, it keeps 10 files of 10 MB.

docs.title: SmartMessage::Logger::Null
docs.text: Discards everything; message blocks are never evaluated. It is what SmartMessage uses when nothing is configured.

docs.title: Per-class loggers
docs.text:
A message class can have its own logger, inherited by its subclasses:

require 'logger'

class PaymentMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  logger Logger.new('log/payments.log')
end

PaymentMessage.logger              # the class logger
PaymentMessage.logger_configured?  # => true (set on the class or an ancestor)
PaymentMessage.reset_logger        # back to the global logger

It receives the lines logged on behalf of that class's messages: creation, publishing and subscription. Transports, the dispatcher, deduplication and the dead letter queue use the global logger.

docs.title: Forcing a logger
docs.text: SmartMessage::Logger.default = logger overrides the configuration until SmartMessage::Logger.reset! (or SmartMessage::Logger.default = nil). It is meant for tests.

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
require 'smart_message'

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.logger    = STDOUT
  config.log_level = :info
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new
end

# messages/ping_message.rb
class PingMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'pinger'
  property :n

  def self.process(message)
    SmartMessage::Logger.default.info('handled a ping', n: message.n)
  end
end

PingMessage.subscribe
PingMessage.new(n: 1).publish
SmartMessage.shutdown

It prints the Subscribed and Published lines from the framework and the handler's own line with its keyword data.

docs.title: Rails
docs.text:
# config/initializers/smart_message.rb
SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.logger = Rails.logger
end

docs.title: Message Deduplication
docs.text:
Deduplication stops a handler from processing the same message twice. A message is identified by the UUID in its header. It is off by default and enabled per message class.

# messages/order_message.rb
class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'order-service'

  ddq_size 500           # optional; default 100
  ddq_storage :memory    # optional; :memory (default) or :redis
  enable_deduplication!

  property :order_id, required: true

  def self.process(message)
    Fulfillment.start(message.order_id)
  end
end

The settings are inherited by subclasses. disable_deduplication! turns it off for a class.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• One queue per handler per message class. The deduplication queues (DDQs) belong to the dispatcher. OrderMessage handled by OrderMessage.process has one queue; the same message class handled by a second handler has another. A message that one handler has seen is still delivered to the others.
  • Reserve before the handler runs. When a message is routed, the dispatcher atomically records its UUID in the handler's queue. If the UUID was already there, the handler is skipped and the duplicate counter is incremented. Because the reservation is made before the handler starts, a second copy that arrives while the first is still being processed is skipped too.
  • Release on failure. If the handler raises, or its circuit breaker rejects the call, the reservation is released and the message goes to the dead letter queue. A redelivery or a replay of that message is then processed.
  • A successful handler keeps the reservation, until it is evicted (memory) or expires (Redis).

You do not call anything from the handler. There is no API for marking a message as processed.

The queue is created when the handler subscribes, so a bad configuration (an unreachable Redis server, for instance) fails the subscribe call.

If the queue becomes unavailable later, the dispatcher logs an error and processes the message without deduplication rather than dropping it.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
ddq_size 1000
ddq_storage :memory

A circular buffer of the last ddq_size UUIDs with a Hash index, guarded by a Mutex. When it is full, the oldest UUID is evicted. It lives in one process: other processes, and the same process after a restart, know nothing about it.

Setting Default Meaning ddq_size 100 UUIDs remembered per handler

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
require 'redis'

ddq_storage :redis, redis: Redis.new(url: 'redis://localhost:6379'), ttl: 3600

Each UUID is one Redis key written with SET NX EX, which makes the reservation atomic across every process that shares the Redis server. Use it when several processes run the same handler and must not both process a message.

Option Default Meaning redis: Redis.new A Redis client ttl: 3600 Seconds a UUID is remembered key_prefix: smart_message:ddq Root of the key names; give environments that share a Redis server different prefixes

Storage is bounded by time, not by count: ddq_size is accepted but does not limit the Redis backend.

Keys are named <key_prefix>:<MessageClass>:<handler id>:<uuid>, by default smart_message:ddq:<MessageClass>:<handler id>:<uuid>. Two processes share a record when they run the same named handler for the same message class. Block, proc and lambda handlers get a generated id per subscribe call, so they do not share a record across processes; use a named class method for handlers that must deduplicate across processes.

The Redis backend fails open. If Redis cannot be reached when the queue is created, subscribe raises SmartMessage::Errors::TransportError. If Redis fails later, the error is logged and the message is processed.

docs.title: Statistics and maintenance
docs.text:
OrderMessage.ddq_enabled?   # => true
OrderMessage.ddq_config     # => { enabled: true, size: 500, storage: :memory, options: {} }

OrderMessage.ddq_stats
# => {
#   enabled: true,
#   queues: {
#     "OrderMessage:OrderMessage.process" => {
#       size: 500, storage_type: :memory, implementation: "SmartMessage::DDQ::Memory",
#       current_count: 2, utilization: 0.4, next_index: 2
#     }
#   }
# }

OrderMessage.clear_ddq!     # forget every UUID this class's handlers have seen

SmartMessage::Stats.get('OrderMessage', 'OrderMessage.process', 'duplicate')   # duplicates skipped

ddq_stats returns { enabled: false } for a class without deduplication. queues has one entry per subscribed handler on each of the class's transports.

docs.title: When duplicates happen
docs.text:
• The same message instance is published twice (a retry in application code).
  • A dead letter queue entry is replayed: the replayed message has the original UUID.
  • A message class has two transports and a process subscribes on both.

For the last case the two transports must share the record: give them the same dispatcher (dispatcher: option), or use the Redis backend.

Each call to MessageClass.new creates a new UUID. Two messages with identical content are not duplicates.

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
require 'smart_message'
require 'tmpdir'

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new
  config.dlq_path  = File.join(Dir.mktmpdir, 'dead_letters.jsonl')
end

# messages/charge_message.rb
class ChargeMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'checkout'
  ddq_size 50
  enable_deduplication!

  property :amount, required: true
  property :fail_once

  @attempts = 0

  class << self
    attr_accessor :attempts

    def process(message)
      self.attempts += 1
      raise 'card processor timeout' if message.fail_once && attempts == 1

      puts "charged #{message.amount} (uuid #{message.uuid[0, 8]})"
    end
  end
end

def wait_for_handlers
  dispatcher = ChargeMessage.transport.dispatcher
  sleep 0.05 until dispatcher.status[:in_flight].zero?
end

ChargeMessage.subscribe

# 1. The same message published twice is handled once
charge = ChargeMessage.new(amount: 10)
charge.publish
charge.publish
wait_for_handlers

# 2. A failed handler releases its reservation, so the retry is processed
ChargeMessage.attempts = 0
retried = ChargeMessage.new(amount: 20, fail_once: true)
retried.publish
wait_for_handlers
retried.publish
wait_for_handlers

SmartMessage.shutdown

stats = ChargeMessage.ddq_stats[:queues]['ChargeMessage:ChargeMessage.process']
puts <<~REPORT
  duplicates skipped: #{SmartMessage::Stats.get('ChargeMessage', 'ChargeMessage.process', 'duplicate')}
  UUIDs remembered:   #{stats[:current_count]}
  dead letters:       #{SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.default.size}
REPORT

It charges 10 once and 20 once, reports one duplicate skipped, two UUIDs remembered, and one dead letter (the first, failed attempt at the second charge).

docs.title: Using a queue directly
docs.text:
ddq = SmartMessage::DDQ.create(:memory, 100)

ddq.reserve('uuid-1')     # => true   recorded by this call
ddq.reserve('uuid-1')     # => false  already there
ddq.contains?('uuid-1')   # => true
ddq.release('uuid-1')     # forget it
ddq.stats
ddq.clear

A custom backend subclasses SmartMessage::DDQ::Base and implements reserve, release, contains?, clear and storage_type. reserve and release must be atomic.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
result = message.publish

publish does four things:

  1. Calls validate!. An invalid message raises SmartMessage::Errors::ValidationError and nothing is sent.
  2. Raises SmartMessage::Errors::TransportNotConfigured when the message has no transport.
  3. Sends the message on every configured transport, each one independently.
  4. Returns a SmartMessage::PublishResult, or raises SmartMessage::Errors::PublishError when every transport failed.

docs.title: SmartMessage::PublishResult
docs.text:
One outcome per transport.

Method Returns success? true when every transport accepted the message partial? true when some transports accepted it and some failed failure? true when no transport accepted it outcomes every Outcome, in transport order successful the outcomes that succeeded failed the outcomes that failed errors the exceptions of the failed outcomes message_class the message class name uuid the message UUID to_h { message_class:, uuid:, success:, outcomes: [...] }

Each SmartMessage::PublishResult::Outcome has:

Method Returns transport the transport instance transport_name its short class name, such as "RedisTransport" error the exception, or nil on success success?, failure? to_h { transport:, success:, error: }

A result means "the transport accepted the message". It says nothing about handlers: they run later, on other threads, possibly in other processes.

docs.title: SmartMessage::Errors::PublishError
docs.text:
Raised when every configured transport failed. error.result is the PublishResult, so nothing about the failure is lost.

begin
  message.publish
rescue SmartMessage::Errors::PublishError => e
  e.message                 # => "All transports failed for OrderMessage: RedisTransport: Connection refused ..."
  e.result.failed.size      # => 1
  e.result.errors.first     # the transport's exception
end

With one transport, that is the only failure mode: publish either returns a successful result or raises.

docs.title: Several transports and partial success
docs.text:
A class or instance with several transports publishes to each. When some succeed and some fail, publish does not raise. It returns a result with partial? true, and you decide whether that is acceptable.

result = message.publish

if result.partial?
  result.failed.each do |outcome|
    warn "#{outcome.transport_name} did not get #{result.uuid}: #{outcome.error.message}"
  end
end

Check success? (or partial?) whenever you publish to more than one transport. A caller that ignores the result treats a partial failure as a success.

docs.title: Failed publishes go to the dead letter queue
docs.text:
Each transport that fails, in a partial failure or a total one, has the message written to the dead letter queue with the transport's class name and the error. Replaying the entry publishes the message again.

The transport's own circuit breaker counts the failure. After repeated failures the circuit opens and further publishes on that transport fail immediately with BreakerMachines::CircuitOpenError, which is recorded and dead-lettered like any other publish failure.

Publish counts are kept in SmartMessage::Stats. Only a publish that reached at least one transport is counted:

SmartMessage::Stats.get('OrderMessage', 'publish')

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
One transport that works and one that always fails.

require 'smart_message'
require 'tmpdir'

SmartMessage.configure do |config|
  config.dlq_path = File.join(Dir.mktmpdir, 'dead_letters.jsonl')
end

class BrokenTransport < SmartMessage::Transport::Base
  def do_publish(_message_class, _serialized_message)
    raise SmartMessage::Errors::TransportError, 'the broker is unreachable'
  end
end

# messages/order_message.rb
class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'order-service'
  property :order_id, required: true
end

memory = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new(auto_process: false)
broken = BrokenTransport.new
dlq    = SmartMessage::DeadLetterQueue.default

# Partial success: no exception
OrderMessage.transport([memory, broken])
result = OrderMessage.new(order_id: 'ORD-1').publish

puts <<~REPORT
  success?   #{result.success?}
  partial?   #{result.partial?}
  succeeded: #{result.successful.map(&:transport_name).join(', ')}
  failed:    #{result.failed.map { |outcome| "#{outcome.transport_name} (#{outcome.error.message})" }.join(', ')}
  DLQ size:  #{dlq.size}
REPORT

# Total failure: PublishError
OrderMessage.transport(broken)
begin
  OrderMessage.new(order_id: 'ORD-2').publish
rescue SmartMessage::Errors::PublishError => e
  puts "raised:    #{e.message}"
  puts "DLQ size:  #{dlq.size}"
end

docs.title: Subscribing with several transports
docs.text: MessageClass.subscribe subscribes on every configured transport. If the same message can arrive over two of them, a handler runs twice. Either subscribe on one transport only, or enable deduplication and make the two transports share a dispatcher (dispatcher: option) or use the Redis deduplication backend.

docs.title: Publishing to a transport directly
docs.text: transport.publish(message) encodes and sends one message on one transport. It returns true or raises the transport's own error. It does not validate the message, does not write to the dead letter queue and does not update the publish counter; message.publish does those.

docs.title: Serializers
docs.text:
A serializer turns a message Hash into a String and back. Each transport owns one serializer and uses it for everything it sends and receives.

SmartMessage ships one serializer: SmartMessage::Serializer::Json. It is the default for every transport.

docs.title: The wire format
docs.text:
A message on the wire is one flat JSON object: the message's properties plus the header under _sm_header.

{
  "_sm_header": {
    "uuid": "0b0e6f0c-4f6e-4a57-9b1e-3b6a2a6f2f10",
    "message_class": "OrderMessage",
    "published_at": "2026-11-11T10:15:30.123456-06:00",
    "publisher_pid": 4242,
    "version": 1,
    "from": "order-service",
    "serializer": "SmartMessage::Serializer::Json"
  },
  "order_id": "ORD-1",
  "amount": 99.99
}

Header fields that are nil are left out. Header fields the receiving version does not know are kept in header.extensions and written back out when the message is published again, so an older consumer can pass on a message from a newer publisher without losing them.

docs.title: Type changes on a JSON round trip
docs.text:
JSON has fewer types than Ruby, so a value can come back as a different type. Every shipped transport serializes (the memory transport too, unless you pass serialize: false), so this applies to what handlers receive.

Published as Received as String, Integer, Float, true, false, nil unchanged Time, DateTime ISO 8601 String with microseconds, such as "2026-11-11T10:15:30.123456-06:00" Date ISO 8601 String, such as "2026-11-11" Symbol String BigDecimal String in plain notation, such as "1.0" any other object its to_h (converted the same way) when it has one, else its to_s Hash keys (String or Symbol) Symbol, at every level Array Array, elements converted as above

The encoding is the same in every process, whatever JSON extensions are loaded.

The header's published_at is the exception: it is restored to a Time automatically.

docs.title: Restoring a type with coerce_key
docs.text:
Declare a coercion on the message class. It runs whenever the property is assigned, including when a received message is rebuilt, so the handler sees the type you want.

coerce_key :placed_at, ->(value) { value.is_a?(String) ? Time.parse(value) : value }

The is_a?(String) guard matters: the same coercion also runs on the publishing side, where the value is already a Time.

A complete program:

require 'smart_message'
require 'time'
require 'date'
require 'bigdecimal'

# messages/invoice_message.rb
class InvoiceMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'billing'
  transport SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new

  property :issued_at
  property :due_on
  property :total
  property :status
  property :raw_time
  property :lines

  coerce_key :issued_at, ->(value) { value.is_a?(String) ? Time.parse(value) : value }
  coerce_key :due_on,    ->(value) { value.is_a?(String) ? Date.parse(value) : value }
  coerce_key :total,     ->(value) { value.is_a?(String) ? BigDecimal(value) : value }
  coerce_key :status,    ->(value) { value.respond_to?(:to_sym) ? value.to_sym : value }

  def self.process(message)
    puts <<~RECEIVED
      issued_at: #{message.issued_at.class}   (coerced)
      due_on:    #{message.due_on.class}   (coerced)
      total:     #{message.total.class}   (coerced)
      status:    #{message.status.inspect}   (coerced)
      raw_time:  #{message.raw_time.class}   (no coercion: a String)
      lines:     #{message.lines.inspect}   (keys are Symbols, values converted)
    RECEIVED
  end
end

InvoiceMessage.subscribe
InvoiceMessage.new(
  issued_at: Time.now,
  due_on:    Date.today + 30,
  total:     BigDecimal('99.50'),
  status:    :open,
  raw_time:  Time.now,
  lines:     [{ 'sku' => 'A-1', kind: :widget }]
).publish

SmartMessage.shutdown

For nested structures, coerce the whole property (a lambda that maps over the Array, for example).

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• A message that cannot be encoded raises SmartMessage::Errors::SerializationError. publish records it as that transport's failure.
  • A payload that cannot be decoded raises SmartMessage::Errors::DecodeError. On receive, the payload is stored in the dead letter queue.

Serializers are not wrapped in a circuit breaker.

docs.title: Using the serializer directly
docs.text:
serializer = SmartMessage::Serializer::Json.new

payload = serializer.encode({ order_id: 'ORD-1', placed_at: Time.now })   # => String
serializer.decode(payload)                                                # => { order_id: "ORD-1", placed_at: "2026-..." }

SmartMessage::Serializer::Json.jsonify(:open)        # => "open"
SmartMessage::Serializer.default                     # => SmartMessage::Serializer::Json
SmartMessage::Serializer.for('json')                 # => SmartMessage::Serializer::Json

To encode or decode a whole message with its header, use the transport (transport.encode_message(message), transport.decode_message(payload)) or SmartMessage::Envelope.

docs.title: Writing a serializer
docs.text:
Subclass SmartMessage::Serializer::Base and implement two private methods. do_encode receives a Hash with Symbol keys, including :_sm_header, and returns a String. do_decode receives the String and returns a Hash; the header must come back under _sm_header (String or Symbol key).

Any error they raise is wrapped in SerializationError or DecodeError.

require 'smart_message'
require 'json'

# JSON, indented for people to read
class PrettyJsonSerializer < SmartMessage::Serializer::Base
  private

  def do_encode(message_hash)
    JSON.pretty_generate(SmartMessage::Serializer::Json.jsonify(message_hash))
  end

  def do_decode(payload)
    JSON.parse(payload, symbolize_names: true)
  end
end

# messages/greeting_message.rb
class GreetingMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'greeter'
  transport SmartMessage::Transport::StdoutTransport.new(serializer: PrettyJsonSerializer.new)
  property :text
end

GreetingMessage.new(text: 'hello').publish

A serializer is given to a transport with the serializer: option. Both ends of a transport must use compatible serializers. The file transport expects one message per line, so a serializer used with it must not emit newlines.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
A transport moves serialized messages. SmartMessage ships four:

Name Class Page :memory SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport Memory Transport :stdout SmartMessage::Transport::StdoutTransport Stdout Transport :file SmartMessage::Transport::FileTransport File Transport :redis SmartMessage::Transport::RedisTransport Redis Transport

Transports for NATS, RabbitMQ, named pipes and lanet exist as separate smart_message-transport-* gems; they have not yet been updated for 0.1.0.

docs.title: Delivery semantics
docs.text:
The transports do not offer the same guarantees. Know which one you are using.

Memory Stdout File Redis Reaches subscribers on the same transport instance, in the same process an IO (default $stdout) every process tailing the same file every process subscribed on the same Redis server and namespace, at that moment Crosses processes no only as text on the IO yes yes Subscribing yes only with loopback: true, and only this instance's own messages yes, by polling the file yes Stored optionally, in memory, up to max_messages no yes: the file is the store, and it only grows no A subscriber that starts later sees nothing earlier not applicable sees only new lines, unless read_from_end: false sees nothing earlier A subscriber that is down not applicable not applicable catches up only if it re-reads the file from the start misses the message Guarantee in-process hand-off write-only durable append; each reader delivers each line once per pass over the file at most once

In words:

  • Memory is in-process. publish hands the message to the handlers subscribed on that transport instance in the same process. Nothing leaves the process. Use it for tests and local development.
  • Stdout is write-only. It prints one JSON line per message to an IO. Handlers are called only when the transport was created with loopback: true, and then only for messages published through that same instance.
  • File is append-only JSON Lines. Writers append; readers tail the file with a poller. The file is never trimmed by the transport.
  • Redis is Redis pub/sub, which is at-most-once. Redis does not store published messages: a message reaches the subscribers connected at the moment it is published and nobody else. A process that is down, not yet subscribed, or reconnecting misses it. Pub/sub channels are global to the Redis server, so the db number does not isolate environments; use namespace:.

None of the shipped transports provides queueing with acknowledgement, consumer groups, or routing by pattern. If every message must reach a consumer that may be down, pub/sub is the wrong tool; the file transport, or a transport backed by a durable broker, is closer to what you need.

Whatever the transport, a failure on the way is captured: a publish that fails, a payload that cannot be decoded, and a handler that fails all put the message in the dead letter queue.

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text: You want Use Unit tests, examples, one process Memory To see messages while developing, or pipe them to another program Stdout An audit trail, or simple hand-off between processes on one machine File Live fan-out between processes or machines, where a missed message is acceptable Redis Live delivery plus a record of everything published Redis and File together (see Publishing)

docs.title: Creating a transport
docs.text:
Directly, or by registered name:

SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new(auto_process: false)

SmartMessage::Transport.create(:memory, auto_process: false)
SmartMessage::Transport.create(:stdout)
SmartMessage::Transport.create(:file, file_path: 'log/messages.jsonl')
SmartMessage::Transport.create(:redis, url: 'redis://localhost:6379', namespace: 'staging')

SmartMessage::Transport.available     # => [:memory, :stdout, :file, :redis]
SmartMessage::Transport.create(:nope) # raises ArgumentError

There is no default transport. Assign one to a message class or to the global configuration; see Configuration.

docs.title: Options common to every transport
docs.text: Option Meaning serializer: A serializer instance. Default SmartMessage::Serializer::Json.new. dispatcher: A SmartMessage::Dispatcher to share. Default: a new one for this transport. circuit_breaker: { transport_publish: {...}, message_processor: {...} } overrides; see Circuit Breakers.

docs.title: The transport interface
docs.text: Method Meaning publish(message) Encode and send, inside the transport's circuit breaker. Returns true or raises. Application code normally calls message.publish instead. subscribe(message_class, handler_id, filters) Called by MessageClass.subscribe unsubscribe(message_class, handler_id), unsubscribe!(message_class) Called by MessageClass.unsubscribe / unsubscribe! subscribers Current subscriptions, by message class name connected?, connect, disconnect Connection state. disconnect is safe to call more than once and never closes an IO the transport was handed. transport_circuit_stats, reset_transport_circuits! The publish circuit breaker encode_message(message), decode_message(payload) The envelope codec with this transport's serializer dispatcher, serializer, options Readers

docs.title: Writing a transport
docs.text:
Subclass SmartMessage::Transport::Base and implement do_publish(message_class, serialized_message). Raise on failure; never return a failure value. Hand inbound payloads to receive(message_class, payload); pass nil for the class when your medium has no channels.

You may also override configure (called from initialize), default_options, default_serializer, subscribe / unsubscribe / unsubscribe! (call super, then start or stop listening), connected?, connect and disconnect.

This complete program defines a transport that keeps payloads in an Array and delivers them when asked:

require 'smart_message'

class ArrayTransport < SmartMessage::Transport::Base
  attr_reader :payloads

  def default_options
    { limit: 100 }
  end

  def configure
    @payloads = []
    @lock     = Mutex.new
  end

  def do_publish(message_class, serialized_message)
    @lock.synchronize do
      raise SmartMessage::Errors::TransportError, 'ArrayTransport is full' if @payloads.size >= @options[:limit]

      @payloads << [message_class, serialized_message]
    end
  end

  # Deliver everything stored so far to this transport's subscribers.
  def flush
    pending = @lock.synchronize { @payloads.shift(@payloads.size) }
    pending.each { |message_class, payload| receive(message_class, payload) }
    pending.size
  end
end

SmartMessage::Transport.register(:array, ArrayTransport)

# messages/note_message.rb
class NoteMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'notes'
  transport SmartMessage::Transport.create(:array, limit: 10)
  property :text, required: true

  def self.process(message)
    puts "note: #{message.text}"
  end
end

NoteMessage.subscribe
NoteMessage.new(text: 'first').publish
NoteMessage.new(text: 'second').publish

puts "stored: #{NoteMessage.transport.payloads.size}"
puts "delivered: #{NoteMessage.transport.flush}"

SmartMessage.shutdown

register raises ArgumentError unless the class inherits from SmartMessage::Transport::Base.

docs.title: File Transport
docs.text: SmartMessage::Transport::FileTransport appends each published message to a file, one serialized message per line. With the default serializer the file is JSON Lines.

docs.title: Delivery semantics
docs.text:
• Append-only. Publishing appends one line and flushes it. The transport never rewrites, trims or rotates the file.
  • Readers tail. Subscribing starts one background poller that reads new complete lines every poll_interval seconds and delivers each to the handlers of the message class named in that line's header.
  • Several processes can share one file. Writers append, readers tail. Every reader sees every line; there is no competition between readers and no acknowledgement.
  • New subscribers start at the end. By default a subscription sees only lines written after it started. With read_from_end: false it reads the whole file first.
  • The read position is in memory. A reader that restarts begins again at the end of the file (or at the beginning with read_from_end: false); it does not resume where it stopped.
  • Truncation is detected. When the file becomes shorter than what a reader has consumed (it was truncated or replaced), the reader starts again from the beginning.
  • A line being written when the poller looks (no newline yet) is left for the next poll.

One file can carry several message classes. A line whose class is loaded in the reading process but has no subscribers there is skipped. So is a line that names a message class the reading process has not loaded: it belongs to another reader. A line that cannot be decoded at all is logged and stored in the reading process's dead letter queue.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
SmartMessage::Transport::FileTransport.new(
  file_path:          'log/messages.jsonl',   # required
  create_directories: true,
  encoding:           nil,
  poll_interval:      0.5,
  read_from_end:      true
)

SmartMessage::Transport.create(:file, file_path: 'log/messages.jsonl')
Option Default Meaning file_path none, required The file, as a String or Pathname; or an IO to write to. Omitting it raises ArgumentError. create_directories true Create the file's directory when the file is first written encoding nil File encoding; nil means Ruby's default poll_interval 0.5 Seconds between checks for new lines; must be a positive number read_from_end true A new subscription sees only lines written after it started; false reads the whole file first

When file_path is an IO, the transport can publish to it but not subscribe from it (subscribe raises SmartMessage::Errors::TransportError), and it never closes it.

transport.path returns the absolute path, or nil for an IO.

docs.title: Connection state
docs.text:
transport.connected?   # => true until disconnect
transport.disconnect   # stops the poller and closes the file the transport opened
transport.connect      # reopens; restarts the poller if there are subscriptions

Publishing after disconnect raises SmartMessage::Errors::TransportError. disconnect is safe to call more than once.

Unsubscribing the last handler stops the poller.

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
One transport writes; a second transport, as another process would, tails the same file.

require 'smart_message'
require 'tmpdir'

path = File.join(Dir.mktmpdir, 'events.jsonl')

# messages/event_message.rb
class EventMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'event-source'
  property :name, required: true

  def self.process(message)
    puts "read from file: #{message.name}"
  end
end

writer = SmartMessage::Transport::FileTransport.new(file_path: path)
reader = SmartMessage::Transport::FileTransport.new(file_path: path, poll_interval: 0.1)

# Subscribe on the reader only
EventMessage.transport(reader)
EventMessage.subscribe

# Publish on the writer only
EventMessage.transport(writer)
EventMessage.new(name: 'started').publish
EventMessage.new(name: 'finished').publish

sleep 0.5                 # give the poller time to see the new lines
reader.disconnect
writer.disconnect
SmartMessage.shutdown

puts "lines in file: #{File.readlines(path).size}"

docs.title: As an audit trail
docs.text:
Because the file is plain JSON Lines, it is easy to inspect:

tail -f log/messages.jsonl | jq '._sm_header.message_class'

To record everything published on another transport, give the message class both:

class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  transport [
    SmartMessage::Transport.create(:redis, namespace: 'production'),
    SmartMessage::Transport.create(:file, file_path: 'log/orders.jsonl')
  ]
end

Note that OrderMessage.subscribe then subscribes on both transports, so a process that both publishes and subscribes would handle each message twice, once from Redis and once from the file. Enable deduplication with a shared dispatcher, or subscribe on one transport only, as the program above does.

docs.title: Replaying a file
docs.text:
Set read_from_end: false to process an existing file from the beginning:

replay = SmartMessage::Transport::FileTransport.new(file_path: 'log/orders.jsonl', read_from_end: false)
OrderMessage.transport(replay)
OrderMessage.subscribe

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text: There is no file rotation, no partitioning by message class, no asynchronous write queue and no named-pipe mode. Rotate the file with an external tool if it must not grow without bound; readers start over from the beginning of the new file when it is shorter than what they had read.

docs.title: Memory Transport
docs.text: SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport keeps everything inside the process. It is meant for tests and local development.

docs.title: Delivery semantics
docs.text:
• In-process only. A published message is delivered to the handlers subscribed on the same transport instance. Nothing is sent to another process.
  • With auto_process: true (the default), publish hands the message to the dispatcher immediately. Handlers run on the dispatcher's thread pool.
  • With auto_process: false, messages are stored and delivered only when you call process_all.
  • Stored messages live in memory, are capped at max_messages (oldest dropped first), and are lost when the process ends.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new(
  auto_process:   true,   # deliver to subscribers on publish
  store_messages: nil,    # keep published messages; default: only when auto_process is false
  max_messages:   1000,   # how many stored messages to keep
  serialize:      true    # encode on publish and decode on delivery
)

SmartMessage::Transport.create(:memory, auto_process: false)
Option Default Meaning auto_process true Deliver to subscribers as part of publish store_messages nil Keep published messages for all_messages and process_all. nil means "only when auto_process is false". max_messages 1000 Upper bound on stored messages; must be a positive Integer serialize true Encode to JSON on publish and decode on delivery, as a real transport does. With false, handlers receive copies of the published object, and type changes caused by serialization go unnoticed.

Leave serialize on in tests: it makes the memory transport behave like the others, so a property that does not survive JSON (a Time, a Symbol) shows up in the test and not in production.

docs.title: Stored messages
docs.text:
transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new(auto_process: false)

transport.all_messages     # => [{ message_class: "OrderMessage", payload: "{...}", published_at: Time }, ...]
transport.messages         # alias
transport.message_count    # => 2
transport.process_all      # deliver every stored message, remove it, return how many
transport.clear_messages   # discard stored messages

payload is the serialized String (or, with serialize: false, a copy of the message object). To get a message back from a stored entry:

entry   = transport.all_messages.first
message = transport.decode_message(entry[:payload])

process_all removes what it delivers, so calling it twice does not deliver anything twice.

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
require 'smart_message'

# messages/order_message.rb
class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'order-service'
  property :order_id, required: true

  def self.process(message)
    puts "processing #{message.order_id}"
  end
end

transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new(auto_process: false)
OrderMessage.transport(transport)
OrderMessage.subscribe

OrderMessage.new(order_id: 'ORD-1').publish
OrderMessage.new(order_id: 'ORD-2').publish

puts "stored before: #{transport.message_count}"   # 2: nothing delivered yet
delivered = transport.process_all
SmartMessage.shutdown                               # wait for the handlers

puts "delivered: #{delivered}, stored after: #{transport.message_count}"

docs.title: In tests
docs.text:
Create a transport per test so that subscriptions and stored messages do not leak between tests:

class OrderMessageTest < Minitest::Test
  def setup
    @transport = SmartMessage::Transport::MemoryTransport.new(auto_process: false)
    OrderMessage.transport(@transport)
  end

  def teardown
    OrderMessage.reset_transport
  end

  def test_publishes_one_message
    OrderMessage.new(order_id: 'ORD-1').publish

    assert_equal 1, @transport.message_count
    assert_equal 'ORD-1', @transport.decode_message(@transport.all_messages.first[:payload]).order_id
  end
end

To test a handler, call it directly with a message (OrderMessage.process(OrderMessage.new(order_id: 'ORD-1'))), or publish with auto_process: true and call transport.dispatcher.shutdown to wait for it.

docs.title: Redis Transport
docs.text: SmartMessage::Transport::RedisTransport uses Redis pub/sub. Each message class is one Redis channel, named after the class and prefixed with the namespace when one is set.

docs.title: Delivery semantics: at most once
docs.text:
Redis pub/sub does not store messages.

  • A message reaches the subscribers that are connected at the moment it is published, and nobody else.
  • A process that is down, has not subscribed yet, or is reconnecting misses the message. There is no replay and no backlog.
  • Every connected subscriber of a channel gets every message (fan-out). There is no load balancing between subscribers and no acknowledgement.
  • Publishing to a channel with no subscribers succeeds; the message is discarded by Redis.

Use this transport when a missed message is acceptable, or pair it with something durable. If every message must arrive, pub/sub is the wrong mechanism.

docs.title: Namespaces, not database numbers
docs.text:
Redis pub/sub channels are global to the Redis server. The db number selects a keyspace for commands such as GET and SET; it does not separate pub/sub channels. Two environments, or two test runs, that share one server see each other's messages even when they use different db numbers.

Use namespace: to keep them apart. It prefixes every channel:

staging = SmartMessage::Transport::RedisTransport.new(namespace: 'staging')
staging.channel_for('OrderMessage')   # => "staging:OrderMessage"

plain = SmartMessage::Transport::RedisTransport.new
plain.channel_for('OrderMessage')     # => "OrderMessage"

For tests, use a namespace that is unique to the run:

require 'securerandom'

transport = SmartMessage::Transport::RedisTransport.new(namespace: "test-#{SecureRandom.hex(4)}")

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
SmartMessage::Transport::RedisTransport.new(
  url:                'redis://localhost:6379',
  db:                 0,
  namespace:          nil,
  reconnect_attempts: 5,
  reconnect_delay:    1,
  subscribe_timeout:  5
)

SmartMessage::Transport.create(:redis, url: ENV.fetch('REDIS_URL'), namespace: 'production')
Option Default Meaning url redis://localhost:6379 Redis URL db 0 Database number, used for commands only. It does not isolate pub/sub. namespace nil Channel prefix: "namespace:ClassName" reconnect_attempts 5 Retries for a lost connection reconnect_delay 1 Seconds between subscriber reconnects subscribe_timeout 5 Seconds to wait for Redis to confirm a subscription

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
The transport uses two connections. One publishes. A second, long-lived connection subscribes; it is opened by the first subscribe and then gains and loses channels with SUBSCRIBE and UNSUBSCRIBE, so changing the set of subscriptions does not drop messages on the channels already subscribed.

subscribe returns once Redis has confirmed the subscription. If Redis does not confirm within subscribe_timeout seconds it raises SmartMessage::Errors::TransportError. A message published after subscribe returns is therefore seen by that subscriber.

When the subscriber connection is lost, the transport logs it, waits reconnect_delay seconds and reconnects, resubscribing every channel, up to reconnect_attempts times. Messages published while it was disconnected are missed. After the last attempt the subscriber stops and the failure is logged; configure a logger so that you can see it. From then on connected? and subscriber_alive? return false, and connect starts the subscriber again.

transport.connected?            # => true when the publishing connection answers PING and the subscriber is running
transport.subscriber_alive?     # => false when the subscriber gave up while channels still have handlers
transport.subscribed_channels   # => ["staging:OrderMessage"]  channels Redis has confirmed
transport.disconnect            # stop the subscriber and close both connections
transport.connect               # reopen (or restart a stopped subscriber), and resubscribe channels that still have handlers

After disconnect, publishing or subscribing raises SmartMessage::Errors::TransportError until connect is called. disconnect is safe to call more than once.

docs.title: What is checked on receive
docs.text: A payload that arrives on a channel is decoded, and the class named in its header must match the channel it arrived on. A mismatch, an unknown class or a payload that is not a SmartMessage envelope is logged and stored in the dead letter queue; the subscription stays alive.

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
This needs a Redis server on localhost:6379.

require 'smart_message'
require 'securerandom'

transport = SmartMessage::Transport::RedisTransport.new(
  url:       ENV.fetch('REDIS_URL', 'redis://localhost:6379'),
  namespace: "example-#{SecureRandom.hex(4)}"
)

# messages/sensor_reading.rb
class SensorReading < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'sensor-7'
  property :celsius, required: true

  def self.process(message)
    puts "reading from #{message.from}: #{message.celsius} C"
  end
end

SensorReading.transport(transport)
SensorReading.subscribe                 # returns once Redis has confirmed

puts "channel: #{transport.subscribed_channels.first}"

SensorReading.new(celsius: 21.5).publish
SensorReading.new(celsius: 22.0).publish

sleep 0.5                               # the messages travel through Redis
transport.disconnect
SmartMessage.shutdown

In a real system the publisher and the subscriber are different processes that use the same url and namespace. Start the subscriber first: a reading published before it subscribes is gone.

docs.title: Deduplication across processes
docs.text: The Redis deduplication backend is independent of this transport. It lets several processes share one record of handled UUIDs, whichever transport delivered the message.

docs.title: Stdout Transport
docs.text: SmartMessage::Transport::StdoutTransport writes each published message to an IO, one serialized message per line. It is useful while developing, for debugging, and for piping messages to another program.

docs.title: Delivery semantics
docs.text:
• Write-only by default. publish prints the message. You can call subscribe, but no handler is ever called, because nothing is read back.
  • With loopback: true, each published message is also delivered to the subscribers of that same transport instance, in the same process.
  • Nothing is stored, and nothing is received from other processes.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
SmartMessage::Transport::StdoutTransport.new                     # writes to $stdout
SmartMessage::Transport::StdoutTransport.new(output: $stderr)
SmartMessage::Transport::StdoutTransport.new(loopback: true)

SmartMessage::Transport.create(:stdout, loopback: true)
Option Default Meaning output nil The IO to write to. nil means whatever $stdout is when the message is published, so output redirected later is respected. Any object with puts works (a StringIO, an open File). loopback false Also deliver published messages to this transport's own subscribers

The transport never closes the IO, because it did not open it. disconnect does nothing.

To write messages to a file by path, use the File Transport.

docs.title: Output format
docs.text:
One line per message: the JSON object the serializer produced, with the message's properties and its header under _sm_header.

{"_sm_header":{"uuid":"0b0e6f0c-...","message_class":"LogMessage","published_at":"2026-11-11T10:15:30.123456-06:00","publisher_pid":4242,"version":1,"from":"my-service","serializer":"SmartMessage::Serializer::Json"},"level":"info","text":"started"}

Because each line is a JSON document, the output works with line-oriented tools such as jq:

ruby my_program.rb | jq 'select(.level == "error") | .text'

docs.title: A complete program
docs.text:
require 'smart_message'

# messages/log_message.rb
class LogMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  from 'my-service'
  transport SmartMessage::Transport::StdoutTransport.new(loopback: true)

  property :level, default: 'info'
  property :text,  required: true

  def self.process(message)
    $stderr.puts "handled: [#{message.level}] #{message.text}"   # stderr keeps stdout pure JSON
  end
end

LogMessage.subscribe
LogMessage.new(text: 'started').publish
LogMessage.new(level: 'error', text: 'disk is full').publish

SmartMessage.shutdown

Standard output gets two JSON lines. Because of loopback: true, the handler also runs for each message and writes to standard error; without it, only the JSON lines would appear.

docs.title: With another transport
docs.text:
Printing every message while also sending it somewhere real is a common use:

class OrderMessage < SmartMessage::Base
  transport [
    SmartMessage::Transport.create(:redis, namespace: 'development'),
    SmartMessage::Transport.create(:stdout)
  ]
end

OrderMessage.subscribe subscribes on both transports, but only the Redis one delivers. See Publishing.
